course.title: Machine Learning, from Models to MLOps
course.description: Fit, evaluate and ship machine-learning models: loss and gradient descent, honest metrics, generalisation, trees and networks, then pipelines, serving and drift monitoring.
course.audience: A capable adult who can write Python and read basic statistics. No prior machine learning is assumed. Plan to take this before ai-engineering, which uses precision, recall and the idea of a held-out set.

paragraphs: A fraud check on a card payment, an estimate of a flat's price and a forecast of which customers will cancel are produced in the same way. A rule with some numbers left open is shown examples whose answers are already known, and the numbers are adjusted until the rule agrees with those examples as closely as it can. That is what machine learning means, and at its smallest it is a straight line fitted to a handful of points, with a slope and an intercept as the only numbers to be chosen.

Choosing the numbers is the easier half of the subject. The harder half is deciding whether the rule will be right about examples it has never seen, and how its mistakes should be counted when one kind of mistake costs far more than the other. Both questions can be settled with arithmetic you can do by hand, so a claimed accuracy becomes something you can check instead of something you have to take on trust.

A model that scores well on a laptop still has to answer real requests within a time limit, from features computed the same way as in training, and it goes on answering after the people and data it learned from have changed. The practice of building, releasing and watching models so that they keep working, usually called MLOps, belongs to the subject as much as the fitting does, because a model that cannot be reproduced or monitored cannot be trusted for long.
outcomes: You'll be able to fit a simple model by hand and read its error.
You'll be able to take gradient descent steps and tune a learning rate.
You'll be able to compute precision, recall, F1 and AUC and choose among them.
You'll be able to diagnose overfitting and prevent leakage.
You'll be able to describe how to reproduce, serve, monitor and govern a model.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Python for Data Analysis, Probability and Statistics, Calculus: Change and Accumulation.

modules.title: Learning from data
modules.description: A model is a function fitted to examples; loss, gradient descent and honest metrics are the three tools that everything else builds on.

modules.title: Models that generalise
modules.description: Why a model that fits its training data can still fail, and the methods that keep it honest: splits, regularisation, good features, trees and networks.

modules.title: From notebook to production
modules.description: The work after the model: reproducible pipelines, serving, monitoring drift, and governing a model that real people depend on.

concepts.title: Model
concepts.summary: A function with adjustable parameters that maps features to a prediction.

concepts.title: Parameters
concepts.summary: The numbers a learning procedure adjusts so that predictions match the training examples.

concepts.title: Residual
concepts.summary: The difference between an observed label and the model's prediction for it.

concepts.title: Loss function
concepts.summary: A single number that scores how wrong the model's predictions are on the data.

concepts.title: Gradient
concepts.summary: The slope of the loss with respect to a parameter, which points towards increasing loss.

concepts.title: Learning rate
concepts.summary: The step size multiplier applied to the gradient on each update.

concepts.title: Confusion matrix
concepts.summary: A table of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

concepts.title: Precision and recall
concepts.summary: Precision is TP/(TP+FP) and recall is TP/(TP+FN).

concepts.title: Base rate
concepts.summary: The share of examples that belong to the positive class.

concepts.title: Decision threshold
concepts.summary: The score above which a classifier predicts the positive class.

concepts.title: ROC curve
concepts.summary: True positive rate plotted against false positive rate across all thresholds.

concepts.title: AUC
concepts.summary: The probability that a random positive scores higher than a random negative.

concepts.title: Overfitting
concepts.summary: Fitting noise in the training set so that error on new data is much worse than error on training data.

concepts.title: Validation set
concepts.summary: Held-out data used to choose between models or settings.

concepts.title: Test set
concepts.summary: Held-out data used once, at the end, to estimate performance on new data.

concepts.title: Regularisation
concepts.summary: Adding a penalty on parameter size to the loss so that the fit prefers simpler models.

concepts.title: Cross-validation
concepts.summary: Rotating which fold is held out so every example is used for validation once.

concepts.title: Bias and variance
concepts.summary: Bias is error from wrong assumptions; variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample.

concepts.title: Scaling
concepts.summary: Rescaling a numeric feature, for example to zero mean and unit variance or to the range 0 to 1.

concepts.title: One-hot encoding
concepts.summary: Replacing a category by one 0/1 column per level.

concepts.title: Leakage
concepts.summary: Information in training that will not exist at prediction time, or test information used in preparation.

concepts.title: Gini impurity
concepts.summary: 1 minus the sum of squared class proportions in a node.

concepts.title: Bagging
concepts.summary: Training models on bootstrap resamples and combining their votes.

concepts.title: Random forest
concepts.summary: Bagged trees that also consider only a random subset of features at each split.

concepts.title: Neuron
concepts.summary: A weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function.

concepts.title: Activation function
concepts.summary: A nonlinear function such as ReLU or sigmoid applied after the weighted sum.

concepts.title: Backpropagation
concepts.summary: Applying the chain rule backwards through a network to get the gradient of the loss for every parameter.

concepts.title: Pipeline
concepts.summary: A fixed sequence of preparation and training steps run the same way every time.

concepts.title: Experiment tracking
concepts.summary: Recording code version, data version, parameters, seed and metrics for every run.

concepts.title: Reproducibility
concepts.summary: Getting the same result again from the same recorded inputs.

concepts.title: Online serving
concepts.summary: Answering one request at a time within a latency budget.

concepts.title: Train-serve skew
concepts.summary: A difference between how features are computed in training and in production.

concepts.title: Canary release
concepts.summary: Sending a small share of traffic to a new model before a full rollout.

concepts.title: Data drift
concepts.summary: A change in the distribution of input features.

concepts.title: Concept drift
concepts.summary: A change in the relation between features and the label.

concepts.title: Population stability index
concepts.summary: Σ (actual% − expected%)·ln(actual%/expected%) across bins.

concepts.title: Demographic parity difference
concepts.summary: The gap between groups in the rate of positive decisions.

concepts.title: Model card
concepts.summary: A short document stating intended use, data, metrics by group and limits.

concepts.title: AI RMF functions
concepts.summary: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.

lessons.title: What a model learns from examples

lead.text: Each of the four students in the figure is one **example**: the hours studied is the **feature**, the input the rule will be given, and the mark scored is the **label**, the value the rule should come close to. A straight line is the simplest rule that can turn a feature into a prediction, and it is written ŷ = w·x + b, where x is the hours studied and ŷ, read as “y-hat”, is the predicted mark. The symbol y without a hat is reserved for the mark that was actually scored.

afterFigure.text: The letters w and b are not fixed. Changing w tilts the line, and changing b slides it up or down, so every pair of values gives a different rule from the same family. A rule of this kind, with a fixed shape and some numbers left open, is a **model**, and the open numbers are its **parameters**. *Learning* is the choice of parameter values that make the rule agree with the examples, which here means choosing two numbers and nothing else.

diagram.caption: Four students, each a point: hours studied across, marks scored up. Use the buttons to mark the fifth student.

lead.text: Take the rule ŷ = 2x, which has w = 2 and b = 0. For the student who studied 3 hours it predicts 6 marks, while the student actually scored 3, so the prediction is 3 marks too high.

afterFigure.text: The gap is defined as the label minus the prediction, y − ŷ, and it is called the **residual**. It is positive when the rule predicts too low and negative when it predicts too high, so the student above has a residual of 3 − 6 = −3.

reveal.text: The residual is positive here, which means the rule predicts too low for this student.

lead.text: One number is needed to compare rules, and adding the residuals themselves does not work, because the positive and negative ones cancel. Squaring each residual first removes the signs, and it also makes one large miss count for more than several small ones, since a miss of 2 contributes 4 while two misses of 1 contribute only 2 between them.

afterFigure.text: The total of the squared residuals is the **sum of squared residuals**, and for the three rules in the figure it is 15, 5 and 1.5. Dividing by the number of examples gives the **mean squared error**, which for the best rule is 1.5 ÷ 4 = 0.375. **Least squares** is the choice of parameters that makes the sum as small as it can be.

lead.text: A straight line has a direct answer. First find the mean of the hours, x̄, and the mean of the marks, ȳ. Then measure how far each example lies from those means and combine the distances in two sums, **Sxy** = Σ (x − x̄)(y − ȳ) and **Sxx** = Σ (x − x̄)².

afterFigure.text: The best parameters are then w = Sxy ÷ Sxx and b = ȳ − w·x̄. The second formula says that the best line passes through the point (x̄, ȳ), the centre of the examples, and the first sets how steeply it tilts there.

steps.headline: Fit the line to the four students: (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 3) and (4, 6).

workedSteps.text: Multiply the distances from the means example by example and add them: (−1.5)(−2.25) + (−0.5)(−0.25) + (0.5)(−0.25) + (1.5)(2.75).
The squared distances of the hours from their mean are 2.25, 0.25, 0.25 and 2.25.
Divide to get the slope, and then find the intercept.
The fitted model is ŷ = 1.5x − 0.5. Its predictions are 1, 2.5, 4 and 5.5, its residuals are 0, 0.5, −1 and 0.5, and its squared residuals add up to 1.5.

steps.headline: Fit a line to three other students: (1, 3), (2, 5) and (3, 10).

workedSteps.text: The means are x̄ = 2 and ȳ = 6.
The distances of the hours from their mean are −1, 0 and 1, so Sxx is 2.
The distances of the marks from their mean are −3, −1 and 4.
Then w = Sxy ÷ Sxx and b = ȳ − w·x̄ give the fitted line.

lead.text: Once w = 1.5 and b = −0.5 have been found, the four examples are no longer needed to make a prediction. A student who studied 5 hours gets ŷ = 1.5 × 5 − 0.5 = 7 marks from the rule alone. This is what makes a model useful: it covers cases that were never listed.

afterFigure.text: It also means that fitting discards information, since four pairs have been reduced to two numbers. The line is a description of *these* four students, and a good fit to them does not show that marks follow hours by a law.

The rule still produces a number, and whether that number is trustworthy is a different question that the later lessons on generalisation take up.

lessons.reviewLabel: What a model learns from examples
lessons.nextAction: Say how a program can find good parameters by taking small steps downhill on a loss, instead of using a formula.

blocks.text: Suppose you have four pairs of numbers: students who studied for 1, 2, 3 and 4 hours scored 1, 3, 3 and 6 marks on a short quiz. A fifth student has studied for 5 hours and has not yet taken the quiz, and you would like a number to expect. The four pairs do not say what the fifth score will be, but they do show a pattern, since more hours went with more marks, and a pattern of that kind can be written as a rule that turns hours into a predicted mark.
Machine learning is the practice of finding such a rule from examples instead of writing it by hand.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to fit a line to a handful of points by hand, predict from it, and work out its error.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later method in the course is a more elaborate version of this one.

recap.keyIdea: A model is a rule with adjustable parameters, and least squares picks the parameters that make the squared residuals add up to the smallest total.

blocks.text: You wrote a straight line as ŷ = w·x + b, measured its error on each example as a residual, and found that squaring and adding the residuals gives one number by which rules can be compared. For a line the best w and b follow from the means and from Sxy and Sxx, and what remains afterwards is just the two parameters.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson finds the same kind of parameters without a formula, by taking small steps downhill on the error, which is the method that also works for models that have no formula.

lessons.title: Loss and gradient descent

lead.text: The first step is to score any candidate with a single number, and for the model ŷ = w·x the score used here is **L(w) = ½ Σ (w·xᵢ − yᵢ)²**, half the sum of the squared residuals. This number is called the **loss**. The ½ is there only so that the factor 2 produced by differentiating the square disappears later.

afterFigure.text: Take the two examples (1, 1) and (2, 3). At w = 0 the predictions are 0 and 0, the residuals are 1 and 3, and the loss is ½(1 + 9) = 5. Every value of w has a loss, so the loss is a curve, and the best w is the bottom of it.

diagram.alt: A parabola showing the loss of the model y-hat equals w times x on the points (1, 1) and (2, 3), lowest near w equal to 1.4. One point is marked on it in each view: loss 5 at w equal to 0, loss 0.5 at w equal to 1, and loss 6.5 at w equal to 3.
diagram.caption: The loss for each value of w, on two points. Use the buttons to see the loss at three values of w.

lead.text: Standing at w = 0, a program cannot see the whole curve, but it can measure how the loss changes when w moves by a small amount. That rate of change is the derivative of the loss, which for a model with one parameter is called the **gradient**. For this loss, differentiating ½(w·xᵢ − yᵢ)² gives xᵢ(w·xᵢ − yᵢ), so **dL/dw = Σ xᵢ(w·xᵢ − yᵢ)**. At w = 0 on the examples (1, 1) and (2, 3) it equals 1·(0 − 1) + 2·(0 − 3) = −7.

afterFigure.text: The sign carries the information. A slope of −7 means that the loss *falls* as w increases, so the minimum lies to the right. A positive slope, as in the third view, means that the loss rises as w increases, so the minimum lies to the left, and a slope of 0 marks the bottom. The gradient therefore points in the direction in which the loss increases, which is away from the minimum, and the size of the slope says how steep the curve is at that point.

diagram.alt: The same loss parabola with an orange tangent line at three values of w. At w equal to 0 the slope is minus 7 and the line falls to the right, at w equal to 1.4 the slope is 0 and the line is flat at the bottom, and at w equal to 2.5 the slope is 5.5 and the line rises.
diagram.caption: The slope of the loss at three values of w. It is negative left of the lowest point, zero at it, and positive right of it.

reveal.text: The gradient is positive, which says that w = 2 sits to the right of the minimum, and that agrees with the minimum being near 1.4.

lead.text: Because the gradient points uphill, a step that lowers the loss goes the opposite way, and the update is **w ← w − η · gradient**. The Greek letter η, read “eta”, is the **learning rate**, a number chosen by you that decides how much of the gradient to use. Repeating the update, with the gradient measured again at each new w, is **gradient descent**.

afterFigure.text: The learning rate scales the step, so the same slope gives a short step when η is small and a long one when it is large.

steps.headline: Take two steps from w = 0 on the examples (1, 1) and (2, 3), with learning rate η = 0.1.

workedSteps.text: Find the gradient at w = 0.
Subtract η times the gradient from w. Since the gradient is negative, subtracting it raises w.
At w = 0.7 the residuals are −0.3 and −1.6, so the loss has fallen from 5 to ½(0.09 + 2.56) = 1.325.
The new gradient is 1·(−0.3) + 2·(−1.6) = −3.5, half as large as before, so the second step is half as long.
The loss is now about 0.406, and the minimum at w = 1.4 is 0.35 away.

steps.headline: Take one step from the other side of the minimum: start at w = 3, with η = 0.1.

workedSteps.text: At w = 3 the residuals are 3 − 1 = 2 and 6 − 3 = 3.
The gradient weights each residual by its x, so it is 1·2 + 2·3.
The gradient is known, so w can now take its step.

reveal.text: The minimum is at 1.4, and w = 2.8 is exactly as far past it as w = 0 was short of it, so the next step would land back on 0.

lead.text: On these two examples the gradient is 5w − 7, so each update gives w − η(5w − 7), and the distance from the minimum is multiplied by **1 − 5η** at every step. With η = 0.02 that factor is 0.9, so the program creeps and needs dozens of steps. With η = 0.1 it is 0.5, and the distance halves each time. With η = 0.2 it would be 0 and the first step would land on the minimum, a coincidence of this loss alone.

afterFigure.text: Beyond that the factor turns negative, which means each step crosses to the far side of the minimum. At η = 0.4 the factor is −1, so w bounces between 0 and 2.8 and never settles, and at η = 0.5 it is −1.5, so every step lands *farther* away and the loss grows. The largest safe rate for this loss is a property of the data, here 2 ÷ Σxᵢ² = 0.4, and in practice a learning rate is found by trying a few values and watching the loss.

diagram.alt: The loss parabola with the dots visited by gradient descent from w equal to 0 under four learning rates: 0.02 creeps slowly, 0.1 halves its distance from the minimum each step, 0.4 jumps to the far side and back forever, and 0.5 lands further away each time and leaves the plot.
diagram.caption: Steps from w = 0 on the same loss under four learning rates. The first two descend, the third bounces, and the fourth climbs out.

reveal.text: The gradient was correct, and the same sign arithmetic worked at η = 0.1. Only the size of the step changed.

lead.text: In 1951 Herbert Robbins and Sutton Monro showed how to use gradient descent when the gradient is only estimated from a random sample of the data, the idea behind the *stochastic* methods that train large models today.

afterFigure.text: With two parameters the loss is a bowl in three dimensions, and with millions it is a surface that cannot be drawn, yet the rule for moving downhill is unchanged. What changes is that the surface may have more than one low point and that the best learning rate depends on how steep the surface is in each direction, which is why training such models involves a good deal of trial.

reveal.text: For this data the factor is 1 − 10η = −1.5, so the loss would grow at every step. The safe rate shrinks as the inputs grow, here to below 0.2.

lessons.orientation: Take gradient descent steps by hand on a one-parameter model and explain how the learning rate changes the result.
lessons.nextAction: Score a classifier with counts of right and wrong decisions, and see why accuracy alone can mislead.

blocks.text: The best slope in the last lesson came out of a formula, but the question behind it can be asked without one. Of all the values of w in ŷ = w·x, which gives the smallest loss, here half the sum of squared residuals? On the two examples (1, 1) and (2, 3), w = 0 gives a loss of 5, while w = 1 gives 0.5. Trying values like this does find the minimum, but it stops being possible once a model has more than a few parameters, because the number of combinations to try grows far too quickly.

The alternative is to stand at one value of w, work out which way the loss slopes there, take a step downhill, and repeat from the new value. This procedure is called **gradient descent**, and it needs nothing from the model except that slope, which is why the same loop trains a straight line with one parameter and a network with billions.

diagram.alt: A parabola showing the loss of the model y-hat equals w times x on the points (1, 1) and (2, 3), lowest near w equal to 1.4. One point is marked on it in each view: loss 5 at w equal to 0, loss 0.5 at w equal to 1, and loss 6.5 at w equal to 3.
diagram.caption: The loss for each value of w, on two points. Use the buttons to see the loss at three values of w.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to take gradient descent steps by hand and say how a learning rate that is too large changes the result.
intro.whyItMatters: It is the update rule behind almost every trained model.

recap.keyIdea: A loss scores the parameters with one number, the gradient gives its slope, and gradient descent steps against that slope by a learning rate that must be small enough not to overshoot.

blocks.text: You scored a model with a loss, measured its slope as the gradient, and updated w by subtracting η times that gradient, which lowered the loss at each step on the examples you used. The learning rate decided how far each step went, and on these examples every rate above 0.4 made the steps bounce or grow instead of settle.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to models that answer yes or no, and to the counts of right and wrong answers that tell you whether such a model can be trusted.

lessons.title: Classification and the confusion matrix

lead.text: Call fraud the **positive** class, since it is the thing being looked for. Then each payment has an actual label and a decision, and two of the four combinations are correct: a flagged payment that really is fraud, a **true positive**, and a payment correctly let through, a **true negative**.

afterFigure.text: The other two are the errors. A payment that is let through although it is fraud is a **false negative**, and a legitimate payment that is flagged is a **false positive**. Counting payments in the four groups gives a table called the **confusion matrix**, and the second view of the figure fills it for 1,000 payments, in which 50 are fraud, the filter flags 40, and 30 of those are really fraud.

diagram.alt: A two by two table. Rows are what is actually true, fraud or fine. Columns are what the model decides, flag or let through. The four cells are true positive, false negative, false positive and true negative. The second view fills them with 30, 20, 10 and 940.
diagram.caption: The four outcomes for a fraud filter. Use the buttons to see their names and then the counts for 1,000 payments.

reveal.text: Flagged payments are those in the first column, the true positives together with the false positives.

lead.text: The simplest score takes the two correct cells and divides by everything: **accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ (TP + TN + FP + FN)**. For the 1,000 payments this is (30 + 940) ÷ 1,000 = 0.97, so the filter is right on 97 payments in every 100.

afterFigure.text: Accuracy treats a missed fraud and a falsely flagged customer as one error each, although one costs the bank a payment and the other costs a customer a phone call, and it says nothing about how many frauds were found.

reveal.text: It lands only a few points below the working filter's 0.97, and it has not found a single fraud.

lead.text: The share of examples that belong to the positive class is the **base rate**, here 50 in 1,000, or 5%. A model that always answers with the majority class is the **baseline**, and its accuracy is 1 minus the base rate, 0.95.

afterFigure.text: The working filter scores 0.97 against a baseline of 0.95, so its extra skill is worth only two points of accuracy, and the two points hide the work it does on the 5 dots that matter. Accuracy gets less informative as the base rate gets more extreme: at a base rate of 1 in 1,000 the baseline is already 0.999.

diagram.alt: A grid of 100 dots where each dot stands for 10 of 1,000 payments. The first view colours the 5 dots that are actually fraud. The second colours the 4 dots the filter flags. The third shows all four outcomes: 3 caught, 2 missed, 1 falsely flagged and 94 correctly cleared.
diagram.caption: The same 1,000 payments in three views. Fraud is a small share of the grid, so most of the dots are correct negatives.

lead.text: Each measure takes one row or column of the matrix. **Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP)** looks only at the payments the filter flagged and asks what share of them were fraud, which is 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75. **Recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN)** looks only at the actual frauds and asks what share the filter caught, which is 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60. The two are different questions: a filter that flags one payment, a certain fraud, has precision 1 and finds almost nothing.

afterFigure.text: A single number that is high only when both are high is the **F1 score**, the harmonic mean of the two, F1 = 2·P·R ÷ (P + R). Here it is 2 × 0.75 × 0.60 ÷ 1.35 = 0.667, which equals 2·TP ÷ (2·TP + FP + FN) = 60 ÷ 90. The harmonic mean sits closer to the smaller of the two values than the ordinary average of 0.675 does, which is why a filter cannot lift F1 by excelling at one measure and neglecting the other.

reveal.text: Recall looks only at the payments that really are fraud, which are the true positives together with the false negatives.

steps.headline: Work out precision, recall and F1 for the fraud filter with TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 20 and TN = 940.

workedSteps.text: Precision uses the flagged payments, TP + FP = 30 + 10.
Recall uses the actual frauds, TP + FN = 30 + 20.
F1 is the harmonic mean of the two.
The accuracy of 0.97 was well above all three, because it also counts the 940 easy negatives.

steps.headline: Work out F1 for a filter on 100 payments with TP = 18, FP = 6, FN = 2 and TN = 74.

workedSteps.text: The filter flagged 24 payments, 18 of them fraud, and there were 20 frauds in all.
Of the 20 frauds, the filter found 18.
F1 combines the two as their harmonic mean.

lead.text: Recall and precision are traded against each other, and the right balance comes from what each error costs. When a missed case is expensive, as when a screening test fails to flag a disease, recall is the measure to raise, and some false alarms are accepted. When a false alarm is expensive, as when every flagged account is frozen, precision matters more. F1 is a reasonable single score when the two errors cost about the same, and accuracy is fair only when the classes are close to balanced.

reveal.text: The measure that counts false alarms among the flagged messages is the one that falls with every false positive.

lead.text: The screening model itself has an accuracy of 0.99.

reveal.text: The baseline scores higher than the model, so the model's accuracy of 0.99 is evidence against it and not for it. Its recall and precision would need to be looked at before it could be trusted.

lessons.orientation: Compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from a confusion matrix and say why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.
lessons.nextAction: Move a decision threshold and see how precision, recall and the ROC curve change for a model that outputs scores.

blocks.text: A fraud filter checks 1,000 card payments, 50 of which are fraudulent, and it is right about 97 payments in every 100. That sounds like a strong result until you count what it did with the 50 frauds: it stopped 30 of them, let the other 20 through, and on top of that flagged 10 honest payments by mistake. A score of 97% describes the filter's work on the 950 honest payments far more than its work on the 50 that matter.

The remedy is to count the two kinds of mistake separately, a fraud that was let through and an honest payment that was stopped, in a table of four cells called the confusion matrix. From those four counts come precision and recall, which say how far the filter's flags can be trusted and how many of the frauds it finds.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from four counts and say when accuracy is the wrong measure.
intro.whyItMatters: These measures are what later lessons use to compare models honestly.

recap.keyIdea: A confusion matrix separates the two kinds of error, and precision and recall measure the positive class that accuracy lets a lazy model ignore.

blocks.text: You sorted the outcomes of a yes-or-no model into true and false positives and negatives, and computed accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from those counts. On the fraud example accuracy was 0.97 while a filter that did nothing scored 0.95, which is why a model is always compared with the baseline and scored on the class it exists to find.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how the filter's score is turned into a flag, and at what moving that threshold does to the four counts.

lessons.title: Thresholds, ROC and AUC

lead.text: Most classifiers do not output a decision directly. They output a score, often read as the probability that an example is positive, and the decision is made afterwards by choosing a **threshold** and flagging every example whose score is at or above it.

afterFigure.text: Moving the threshold moves examples between the cells of the confusion matrix. Because the matrix changes, so do precision and recall, which means a classifier does not have *one* precision and *one* recall but a pair for each threshold.

At threshold 0.8 two examples are flagged, both positive. At 0.6 four are flagged, three positive and one negative. At 0.4 six are flagged, four positive and two negative.

reveal.text: Three of the flagged examples are positive and two are negative, which is the lowest precision reached so far while the recall holds at 0.75.

lead.text: Working down the sorted list gives the pair of measures at each threshold. At 0.8 the filter has 2 true positives and no false positives, so precision is 1 and recall is 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5. At 0.7 a false positive enters, and precision falls to 0.667 with recall unchanged. At 0.6 a true positive is added and both measures read 0.75, and at 0.4 recall reaches 1 while precision is 0.667.

afterFigure.text: Recall can only rise as the threshold falls, since flagging more examples never loses a positive, while precision rises and falls irregularly. The third measure needed is the **false positive rate**, FPR = FP ÷ (FP + TN), the share of the actual negatives that were flagged; recall is also called the **true positive rate**, TPR, when it is plotted against it. At 0.4 the FPR is 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5.

reveal.text: Every negative is flagged and so is every positive. The opposite extreme, a threshold above 0.92, flags nothing and gives a rate of 0, and the curve between them is the subject of the next screen.

lead.text: Each threshold gives one pair, (FPR, TPR), and a point on a plot with FPR across and TPR up. Starting with a threshold above every score gives the point (0, 0), where nothing is flagged. Lowering the threshold past each score in turn moves the point up when that score belongs to a positive and right when it belongs to a negative, until a threshold below every score reaches (1, 1). The path is the **ROC curve**, short for receiver operating characteristic, a name that comes from its first use in radar signal detection in the Second World War.

afterFigure.text: A model that scored at random would climb along the dashed diagonal, flagging positives and negatives at the same rate. The further the curve bulges above the diagonal towards the top left corner, the better the model separates the two groups, and a curve through the corner (0, 1) means that some threshold finds every positive with no false alarm.

diagram.alt: A square plot of true positive rate against false positive rate with a staircase curve from the bottom left to the top right above the dashed diagonal. A dot marks the curve at threshold 0.7, 0.6 or 0.4: false positive rate 0.25 and true positive rate 0.5, then 0.25 and 0.75, then 0.5 and 1.

lead.text: The curve can be summarised by the area beneath it, called the **AUC**, short for area under the curve. It has a direct meaning: pick one positive example and one negative example, and the AUC is the probability that the model scores the positive higher. For the eight examples there are 4 × 4 = 16 such pairs, and the grid ticks 13 of them. The three misses are the negative at 0.75, which beats the positives at 0.66 and 0.45, and the negative at 0.58, which beats the positive at 0.45.

afterFigure.text: The AUC is therefore 13 ÷ 16 = 0.8125, which the second view confirms as the shaded area. A model that ordered every pair correctly would score 1, a model that ordered them at random would score 0.5, and anything below 0.5 means the ordering is mostly backwards. The AUC depends only on the ordering of the scores, so it does not change if every score is squeezed into a narrower range, and it uses no threshold at all.

reveal.text: Each of the two positives is compared with each of the two negatives, so there are four pairs, and a pair counts when the positive's score is the larger.

steps.headline: Find the point on the ROC curve for threshold 0.6 on the eight examples.

workedSteps.text: The examples with a score of at least 0.6 are 0.92, 0.85, 0.75 and 0.66, of which 0.92, 0.85 and 0.66 are positive.
Four examples are actually positive and four negative, so the rest are the false negatives and true negatives.
The true positive rate is the recall, and the false positive rate uses the actual negatives.
The point (0.25, 0.75) is on the curve, as the second view of the figure shows.

steps.headline: Find the point for threshold 0.2 on the same eight examples.

workedSteps.text: The examples with a score of at least 0.2 are 0.92, 0.85, 0.75, 0.66, 0.58, 0.45 and 0.30, which includes all four positives.
So TPR = 4 ÷ 4 = 1.
That fixes the height of the point, and its position along the bottom of the plot is still to be found.

lead.text: An AUC of 0.9 does not mean that 90% of decisions are right. It means that a random positive outranks a random negative 90% of the time, and the decisions made at a particular threshold can be much better or worse than that, depending on where the threshold is set and on how common the positive class is. The AUC is the right summary when you have not yet decided on a threshold, and the precision and recall at the chosen threshold are what the user experiences afterwards.

afterFigure.text: On data where positives are very rare, the false positive rate can look small while the precision is poor, because the negatives are so numerous: one percent of a million negatives is ten thousand false alarms.

reveal.text: The statement about pairs is exact, and the statements about accuracy and about the share of positives found at a given threshold are different quantities.
The same relationship works in both directions: the AUC is a share of pairs, so a share and a number of pairs determine each other.

lessons.orientation: Move a decision threshold, recompute precision and recall, and compute AUC as the fraction of correctly ordered positive-negative pairs.
lessons.nextAction: Hold some data back and see why a model's score on the examples it was fitted to cannot be trusted.

blocks.text: The scores 0.92, 0.85, 0.75, 0.66, 0.58, 0.45, 0.30 and 0.15 come from a model that has ranked eight examples, and the model has not yet said which of them are positive. Saying so requires a threshold, a score at or above which an example is flagged. At 0.8 two examples are flagged and both are right, while at 0.4 six are flagged and two of those are wrong, so one set of scores gives many different pairs of precision and recall depending on where the line is drawn.

A model is therefore better described by the whole range of choices its scores allow than by any single one. That range can be drawn as a curve, the ROC curve, and the area under it can be found without choosing a threshold at all, by counting how often a positive example is scored above a negative one.

At threshold 0.8 two examples are flagged, both positive. At 0.6 four are flagged, three positive and one negative. At 0.4 six are flagged, four positive and two negative.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to apply a threshold to scores, work out precision and recall, and compute AUC by counting ordered pairs.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing a threshold is a decision about costs, and AUC lets you compare models before making it.

recap.keyIdea: A threshold turns scores into decisions and moves examples between the cells of the matrix, the ROC curve records every threshold at once, and the AUC is the share of positive-negative pairs ordered correctly.

blocks.text: You applied a threshold to a list of scores, found that lowering it raises recall and lets in false positives, and plotted the true positive rate against the false positive rate to draw the ROC curve. The area beneath it equals the share of positive and negative pairs the model orders correctly, which measures ranking, and which is not the same as accuracy.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks a different question of every score so far, which is whether it would hold up on examples the model has never seen.

lessons.title: Generalisation and the test set

reveal.text: A model with as many parameters as examples can match every label, so the error on those examples says nothing about how it will do on others.

lead.text: A polynomial of degree 1, a straight line, misses the wave, and its mean squared error on the ten points is 0.19. Degree 9 has ten parameters, one for each point, so it can pass through all of them, and its error on the points it was fitted to is exactly 0.

afterFigure.text: The error on the examples a model was fitted to is its **training error**, and it can only fall as the model gets more flexible. The degree-9 curve swings far above and below the wave between the points, so nine *new* points from the same wave sit a long way from it. A model that has matched the noise in its examples instead of the pattern under it is **overfitting**.

diagram.alt: Ten noisy training points that follow one cycle of a wave, with a fitted polynomial. Degree 1 is a nearly flat straight line that misses the wave, degree 3 follows the wave closely, and degree 9 passes through every point and swings wildly between them. The fourth view adds nine empty circles, new points from the same wave, that the degree 9 curve misses by a long way.
diagram.caption: Polynomials of degree 1, 3 and 9 fitted to the same ten points. The fourth view adds nine new points the curve was not fitted to.

lead.text: To see the cost directly, hold some examples back and fit the model without them. The error on those held-back examples is the **validation error**, and it estimates how the model will do on data it has not seen. For the nine held-back points the validation error is 0.177 at degree 1, 0.055 at degree 3, and 2.78 at degree 9, which is more than fifteen times the straight line's.

afterFigure.text: The training error falls all the way to zero, while the validation error falls to a minimum at degree 3 and then climbs. The model at degree 1 is **underfitting**, with both errors high because it cannot represent the wave, and the model at degree 9 is overfitting, with a training error of 0 and a validation error that is far larger. The *gap* between the two, validation minus training, is the symptom to look for.

diagram.alt: A line chart of mean squared error against polynomial degree from 1 to 9. The training error falls steadily from 0.19 to 0. In the second view the validation error is added: it falls to 0.055 at degree 3, then rises, and at degree 9 it is 2.78, off the top of the chart.
diagram.caption: Training error and validation error as the model gets more flexible. Use the buttons to add the validation line.

reveal.text: A gap this size says the model has learned things about the training set that do not carry over.

lead.text: Choosing the degree that has the lowest validation error is itself a kind of fitting, with the degree as the parameter, and the validation error of the winner is therefore a little flattering. A third set is held back for that reason. The **training set** is used to fit the parameters, the **validation set** is used to choose settings such as the degree or the learning rate, and the **test set** is used once, at the end, to report how the chosen model is expected to perform.

afterFigure.text: The test set only keeps its value if it is not used to make choices. Each time a result on the test set sends you back to change the model, a little information about those rows leaks into the model, and after many such looks the test score is an optimistic estimate and no longer an honest one.

reveal.text: A fifth of the rows go to validation.

steps.headline: Choose among the three models, using their errors: degree 1 (training 0.19, validation 0.18), degree 3 (0.059, 0.055) and degree 9 (0, 2.78).

workedSteps.text: Compare the models on the validation set, which was not used for fitting. The lowest validation error is 0.055, at degree 3.
Degree 9 has the lowest training error, 0, but also by far the highest validation error, 2.78.
Degree 3 shows almost no gap between its two errors, 0.059 against 0.055, so it is neither badly underfitting nor overfitting.
The test set has not been touched. It will be used once, on degree 3, to report the final figure.

reveal.text: Both scores are low and close together, so the model cannot represent the pattern. A small gap does not make a model good when both scores are poor.

lead.text: The splits above were random, and for examples that do not depend on one another random is the right choice. Monthly sales, sensor readings and transactions do depend on time, because a model will be used to predict what comes *next*. A random split of 24 months scatters the test months among the training months, so the model has seen the months on both sides of each test month, which is information it will never have in use.

afterFigure.text: Splitting by time keeps the future out of training. The first 16 months train the model, the next 4 choose the settings, and the last 4 are the test set. The score on the last 4 months is then a fair preview of deployment, and it is usually lower than the score from a random split, which is a sign that the random split was flattering the model.

lessons.orientation: Split data into training, validation and test sets and diagnose overfitting from the gap between training and validation error.
lessons.nextAction: Add a penalty to the loss so that a flexible model cannot chase noise, and average several validation scores to compare settings.

blocks.text: Ten points that follow one cycle of a wave, with some noise added, can be fitted by a polynomial of any degree. A polynomial of degree 9 has ten parameters, one for each point, so it can be made to pass through all ten, while a straight line has two parameters and misses most of them. Judged by its error on those ten points the degree-9 curve is the better model, yet the points are only a sample of the wave, and the error that matters is the error on points the model has not been given.

How well a model does on examples it has not seen is called **generalisation**, and it can be measured honestly only by keeping some examples out of the fitting. Comparing the error on the examples a model was fitted to with the error on the ones kept back tells you whether it has learned the pattern or the noise.

diagram.alt: A line chart of mean squared error against polynomial degree from 1 to 9. The training error falls steadily from 0.19 to 0.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to split data into three sets, say what each is for, and diagnose overfitting from the gap between two scores.
intro.whyItMatters: Every honest evaluation in machine learning rests on a split like this.

recap.keyIdea: A model is judged on data it was not fitted to, with a validation set to choose settings and a test set kept for a single final look.

blocks.text: You fitted polynomials of rising degree and saw the training error fall to zero while the validation error rose, which is overfitting, and a straight line that was too simple for either error to be small. Settings are chosen on the validation set, the test set is touched once, and time-ordered data is split in time order.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson adds a penalty that discourages the extreme curves, and then repeats the validation split several times so that one lucky split cannot decide the comparison.

lessons.title: Regularisation and cross-validation

lead.text: A way to prevent enormous coefficients is to add the size of the parameters to the loss, so that the model must pay for every large coefficient. With the penalty λ·w² the loss becomes **L(w) = MSE(w) + λ·w²**, where w stands for all the parameters and the penalty adds up their squares, and λ is a number you choose that sets the price.

afterFigure.text: Penalising the squares of the parameters is called **L2 regularisation**, and in linear models ridge regression. With no price the curve swings and misses the new points, with a small price of λ = 0.00001 it follows the wave and the validation error falls from 2.78 to 0.063, and with a large price it flattens and underfits.

diagram.alt: The degree 9 polynomial fitted to the same ten points three times with a growing penalty on its coefficients. With no penalty it swings wildly and the nine new points are far from it. With a small penalty it follows the wave closely. With a large penalty it is a shallow curve that misses the wave. Training and validation errors are printed under each.
diagram.caption: The same ten points and the same degree-9 model with three penalty strengths. Filled dots were fitted; empty dots are held back.

reveal.text: The penalty is positive whatever the sign of w, since w is squared.

lead.text: Go back to the loss of the second lesson on the points (1, 1) and (2, 3), whose mean squared error is 2.5w² − 7w + 5 and whose best w is 1.4. Adding λw² gives (2.5 + λ)w² − 7w + 5, and the best w becomes **w = 3.5 ÷ (2.5 + λ)**. With λ = 0.5 it is 1.167, and with λ = 2.5 it is 0.7. A bigger λ pulls w towards zero, which is why this is also called *shrinkage*.

afterFigure.text: The training error pays for this. The mean squared error at the best w is 0.1 with no penalty, about 0.236 at λ = 0.5 and 1.325 at λ = 2.5, so **regularisation always makes the fit to the training data worse**. It helps only when the stability it buys is worth more than the fit it costs, and that is judged on validation data.

lead.text: The penalty can be built from absolute values instead of squares, so that the loss is **MSE(w) + λ·|w|**, called **L1 regularisation**. On the same example the best w is (7 − λ) ÷ 5 while that is positive, and it reaches exactly 0 when λ is 7 and stays there.

afterFigure.text: The difference matters when a model has many features. An L1 penalty can switch useless features off completely, leaving a model that uses only a few, while an L2 penalty keeps all of them with small coefficients.

diagram.alt: A plot of the best value of w against penalty strength lambda for the loss of the earlier lesson on the points (1, 1) and (2, 3). With an L2 penalty w shrinks smoothly from 1.4 and never reaches zero. With an L1 penalty w falls in a straight line and is exactly zero from lambda equal to 7. The third view draws both.
diagram.caption: How the best w shrinks as the penalty grows. Use the buttons to compare the two kinds of penalty.

reveal.text: The absolute value of −3 is 3, so the sign of the parameter does not change the penalty.
Every row sits in exactly one fold, so it is scored once and is used for training in the other four rounds.

lead.text: A single validation split can be lucky or unlucky, because the score depends on which rows happened to land in it. **K-fold cross-validation** removes that by averaging. The data is cut into k equal **folds**, and for each fold in turn the model is fitted on the other k − 1 folds and scored on the held-out one. With k = 5 the figure shows five rounds, and for 2,500 rows each round trains on 2,000 and scores on 500.

afterFigure.text: The five scores are then averaged: 0.78, 0.80, 0.76, 0.79 and 0.77 have a mean of 0.78. The result is an *estimate* of how a setting performs, used to choose between settings such as λ or the degree. It does not produce a final model, since the five fitted models are discarded, and after choosing, the model is fitted again on all the training data.

diagram.alt: Five rows of five boxes. In row one the first box is shaded as the held-out fold, in row two the second, and so on down to the fifth box in row five. The other four boxes in each row are used for training. The second view writes an accuracy beside each row, 0.78, 0.80, 0.76, 0.79 and 0.77, and their mean, 0.78.
diagram.caption: Each row is one round: four fifths of the data train the model and the shaded fifth scores it. Use the buttons to show the five scores.

lead.text: Setting A scores 0.78, 0.80, 0.76, 0.79 and 0.77 across the folds, and setting B scores 0.84, 0.72, 0.80, 0.70 and 0.84. Both average 0.78. A's scores stay within two points of the mean, while B ranges across fourteen points, so B is less predictable: on new data its score could easily land at 0.70 or at 0.84.

afterFigure.text: The spread is measured by the **standard deviation** of the fold scores, here found by dividing the sum of squared deviations by k − 1. When the means agree, the setting with the smaller spread is the safer choice, and when they differ by less than the spread the difference may only be the luck of the folds.

steps.headline: Find the standard deviation of setting A's fold scores: 0.78, 0.80, 0.76, 0.79 and 0.77.

workedSteps.text: The mean is the sum, 3.90, divided by 5.
Subtract the mean from each score: 0, 0.02, −0.02, 0.01 and −0.01.
Square the deviations and add them. Dividing by k − 1 = 4 gives the variance.
The standard deviation is the square root of that variance.

steps.headline: Find the standard deviation of setting B's fold scores: 0.84, 0.72, 0.80, 0.70 and 0.84.

workedSteps.text: The mean is 3.90 ÷ 5.
The deviations are 0.06, −0.06, 0.02, −0.08 and 0.06, and their squares are 0.0036, 0.0036, 0.0004, 0.0064 and 0.0036.
That leaves the variance and then the standard deviation still to be found.

lead.text: A model that is too stiff to represent the pattern is wrong in the same way whichever sample it sees, an error called **bias**, and it underfits. A model that is flexible enough to follow the noise in its sample gives quite different fits on different samples, an error called **variance**, and it overfits. The penalty strength moves a model along this scale: with none the degree-9 curve has high variance, and with a large one it has high bias.

diagram.alt: The training and validation errors of the degree 9 model as the penalty strength grows from 0 to 10. Training error rises steadily. Validation error is huge with no penalty, falls to a minimum near 0.00001, and then climbs again as the model becomes too stiff. The left side is labelled variance and the right side bias.
diagram.caption: Training and validation error against penalty strength. The lowest validation error lies between a model that fits the noise and one that is too stiff.

reveal.text: A stronger penalty makes the fit to the training data worse and the model's behaviour more stable.
Every parameter adds its own square to the penalty, so a model with many parameters pays for all of them together.

lessons.orientation: Add an L2 or L1 penalty to a loss, and average a metric over k folds to compare two models.
lessons.nextAction: Prepare input features, scale them, and keep information from the validation rows out of the preparation.

blocks.text: Fitted to ten points with no restriction, a degree-9 polynomial has a largest coefficient of about 2.9 million, and its error on nine new points is 2.78. Add a charge for the size of the coefficients to the loss, and with a price of 0.00001 per unit of squared coefficient the same model follows the wave, with an error of 0.063 on the new points. The charge costs the model some accuracy on the training points, and the new points are better for it.

Choosing the price is itself a decision that has to be made on data the model was not fitted to, and a single validation split is a thin basis for it. A penalty sets the price, and the repeated split, cross-validation, makes the choice more reliable.

diagram.alt: The degree 9 polynomial fitted to the same ten points three times with a growing penalty on its coefficients. With no penalty it swings wildly and the nine new points are far from it. With a small penalty it follows the wave closely. With a large penalty it is a shallow curve that misses the wave. Training and validation errors are printed under each.
diagram.caption: The same ten points and the same degree-9 model with three penalty strengths. Filled dots were fitted; empty dots are held back.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to add an L2 or L1 penalty to a loss and average a score over folds to compare two settings.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every practical model has a penalty strength or similar setting that has to be tuned this way.

recap.keyIdea: A penalty on the parameters trades some training fit for stability, and k-fold cross-validation estimates which strength gives the best result on unseen data.

blocks.text: You added λ·w² or λ·|w| to a loss, saw that the best w shrinks as λ grows and that the training error pays for it, and averaged five fold scores to estimate how a setting performs. The strength that minimises validation error sits between too much variance and too much bias, and when the means are equal the spread decides.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the inputs of a model, where scaling and encoding must be done without letting the validation rows influence the preparation.

lessons.title: Features, scaling and leakage

lead.text: A model that sees a flat's floor area in square metres, between 40 and 120, and its number of rooms, between 1 and 5, is comparing numbers of very different sizes, and methods that take steps along the features, such as gradient descent, or measure distances between rows are dominated by the larger one. **Min-max scaling** maps the smallest value to 0 and the largest to 1 with **(x − min) ÷ (max − min)**, so that for the floor areas 40, 50, 60, 80 and 120 the value 50 becomes 10 ÷ 80 = 0.125.

afterFigure.text: **Standardising** instead subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, **z = (x − μ) ÷ σ**, which gives the value in units of standard deviations from the mean. What matters is that μ, σ, min and max are *numbers computed from a particular set of rows*.

diagram.alt: Five dots on a number line for five flats with floor areas 40, 50, 60, 80 and 120 square metres. The first view shows the raw areas. The second view rescales them with min-max to 0, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 and 1. The third standardises them to minus 1.06, minus 0.71, minus 0.35, 0.35 and 1.77. The pattern of spacing is the same in all three.
diagram.caption: The same five values on three scales. The dots keep their relative positions, and only the numbers change.

reveal.text: Min-max scaling needs the smallest and largest values of the whole column, and not only the value being scaled.
The median is the middle value when they are in order, and the one large value does not move it.

lead.text: Most models cannot accept a gap, so the gap is **imputed**, filled with a stand-in. The usual stand-ins are a typical value of the column. For the five values 2, 3, 5, 6 and 84 the mean is 20, a figure that none of the first four values comes near, because the single 84 pulls it up, while the median is 5.

afterFigure.text: The median is therefore the safer choice for a skewed column, and the mean is fine when the values are spread evenly. Like a scaling rule, the median is computed from a set of rows, and it should come from the training rows only.

lead.text: Models need numbers, and a text column such as the way a person travelled, with the four levels bike, bus, car and walk, has to be converted. Giving the levels integer codes 1 to 4 looks economical, but it tells the model that a walk is four times a bike and that a car is exactly halfway between a bus and a walk, relations that mean nothing here. **One-hot encoding** avoids this by giving each level its own column that holds 1 when the row has that level and 0 otherwise.

afterFigure.text: The set of levels, like a mean, is something learned from the rows that were seen.

lead.text: Leakage is information in the training data that will not be available when the model is used. Suppose a service wants to predict which customers will cancel, and one column, the cancellation reason, is filled in when a customer cancels. For the customers who stayed it is empty, so a model can learn that *any* reason at all means a cancellation, and it will score almost perfectly in testing. This is **target leakage**, because the feature is a consequence of the label.

afterFigure.text: The warning sign is a result that is too good. A feature that predicts the label almost perfectly is rarely a discovery, and it is usually a leak. The test is a question about time: at the moment the prediction would be made, would this column already have its value? If it would only be filled in later, it must be dropped, however much the score falls.

lead.text: The second kind of leakage is quieter. If the scaler is fitted to *all* the rows before the data is split, its mean and standard deviation include the [[test set|Rows held back for one final estimate of performance. Met in 'Generalisation and the test set'.]], so a little information about the test rows has already entered the training data. The fitted numbers must come from the training rows only, and the same numbers are then applied unchanged to the validation and test rows.

afterFigure.text: The effect is usually small for one scaler, and it grows with every step that learns from the data, such as imputing, choosing features or encoding categories. The safe habit is to split first, fit each step on the training part, and *apply* it to the rest. In cross-validation this means refitting the steps inside every fold, which is what a pipeline does.

steps.headline: Min-max scale a test value of 80 using a scaler fitted to the training values 40, 50 and 60.

workedSteps.text: Fit the scaler on the training rows only, which gives its two numbers.
Apply those numbers to the test value.
Compare the leaky version, which fits the scaler on all four values and so lets the test row set the maximum.
The leaky scaler hides that the test row is unlike the training rows, which is a thing the model should discover.

steps.headline: Standardise a test value of 11 using a scaler fitted to the training values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7 and 9.

workedSteps.text: The training mean is 40 ÷ 8.
The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4 and 16, which add up to 32, and 32 ÷ 8 = 4, so the population standard deviation is its square root.
The test value 11 is then put on the same scale, using the training numbers.

reveal.text: The scaler was fitted before the split, so it saw every row.

lessons.orientation: Prepare features with scaling, encoding and imputation, and spot target leakage and preprocessing leakage.

blocks.text: Five flats have floor areas of 40, 50, 60, 80 and 120 square metres. Their mean is 70 and their standard deviation is about 28.28, so the largest is 1.77 standard deviations above the mean, and the same flats described by min-max scaling run from 0 to 1. Each rescaling is a recipe computed from the five numbers that were used.

That last point decides how a model's inputs must be prepared, because every number a scaler, an imputer or an encoder learns comes from some set of rows. If those rows include the ones the model will later be tested on, the test is weakened without any error being raised, and the same happens when a feature carries information that only exists once the answer is known. Knowing where each number in the preparation came from lets you spot both kinds of **leakage** before a score that looks too good reaches anyone else.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to scale, impute and encode a feature, and spot both target leakage and preprocessing leakage.
intro.whyItMatters: Most models that score suspiciously well in a notebook have a leak.

recap.keyIdea: Features are scaled, filled and encoded with numbers learned from the training rows alone, and any column that is only known after the outcome has to be removed.

blocks.text: You rescaled a column by min-max and by standardising, filled a gap with the median of a skewed column, and turned a category into one-hot columns. Each step learned something from a set of rows, so each has to be fitted to the training rows only, and a column recorded after the outcome has to be dropped even though it scores brilliantly.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson builds the decision tree, a model that needs no scaling and chooses its splits by a number computed from counts.

lessons.title: Decision trees and ensembles

lead.text: A decision tree makes a prediction by asking a series of yes-or-no questions about the features. Each question splits the examples into two groups, each group is split again, and a group that is no longer split is a leaf, which predicts the majority class among the examples in it.

afterFigure.text: The measure used by the CART method is the **Gini impurity**, **G = 1 − Σ p²**, where p is the share of each class in the node. A pure node has G = 0. For the node of seven and three, G = 1 − 0.7² − 0.3² = 1 − 0.49 − 0.09 = 0.42, and a node of five and five has the largest possible value for two classes, 0.5.

diagram.alt: Two views of Gini impurity. The first shows three nodes of ten examples each: all ten positive with Gini 0, seven positive and three negative with Gini 0.42, and five of each with Gini 0.5. The second plots Gini against the share of positives as an arch that is 0 at both ends and 0.5 in the middle.
diagram.caption: Gini impurity for nodes of ten examples. Use the buttons to compare three nodes and then see the whole curve.

reveal.text: The node is mostly one class, so its value is well below the 0.5 of an even mix.
The weights are the shares of the examples, one half each, and one child contributes nothing.

lead.text: Each child is weighted by its share of the examples, so a large mixed child counts for more than a small one. The **weighted child impurity** is the sum of each child's share times its Gini, and the **gain**, the impurity decrease, is the parent's Gini minus that sum. For the split on income the left child has 5 of the 10 loans and G = 0, the right child has the other 5 and G = 0.48, so the weighted impurity is 0.5 × 0 + 0.5 × 0.48 = 0.24 and the gain is 0.42 − 0.24 = 0.18.

afterFigure.text: A split on age sends 6 loans left (4 positive, 2 negative, G = 0.444) and 4 right (3 positive, 1 negative, G = 0.375), which gives a weighted impurity of 0.417 and a gain of only about 0.003. The tree takes the question with the largest gain, here income, and then repeats the search inside each child, which is why trees are built greedily, one question at a time.

diagram.alt: A decision tree stump for a node of 10 loans, 7 positive and 3 negative, with Gini 0.42. Split A asks if income is at least 40 thousand and sends 5 positive and 0 negative left and 2 positive and 3 negative right, with weighted Gini 0.24. Split B asks if age is under 30 and sends 4 positive and 2 negative left and 3 positive and 1 negative right, with weighted Gini 0.417.
diagram.caption: Two candidate questions for the same node. The better split leaves the children purer.

steps.headline: Score a third question for the same node: it sends 7 loans left (6 positive, 1 negative) and 3 right (1 positive, 2 negative).

workedSteps.text: The left child has Gini 1 − (6/7)² − (1/7)².
The right child has Gini 1 − (1/3)² − (2/3)².
Weight each child by its share of the 10 loans, 7 out of 10 and 3 out of 10, and add.
Subtract that from the parent's impurity.

steps.headline: Compute the gain of a split on loan term, which sends 8 loans left (6 positive, 2 negative) and 2 loans right (1 positive, 1 negative).

workedSteps.text: The left child has Gini 1 − (6/8)² − (2/8)², and the right has 1 − (1/2)² − (1/2)².
The left child holds 8 of the 10 loans and the right child holds 2.
The gain is then the parent's Gini of 0.42 minus that weighted impurity.

lead.text: Left to run, a tree keeps asking questions until every leaf holds examples of one class, so that its training accuracy is 1, the same condition that made the degree-9 polynomial score zero error and fail on new data. A deep tree has memorised its examples, including the noise in them, and a different sample of the same population would produce a quite different tree.

afterFigure.text: That sensitivity is the variance met in the regularisation lesson, and averaging is a way to reduce it. If many models were each fitted to a different sample and their answers were combined, the quirks of any one would be outvoted.

lead.text: A **bootstrap sample** is made by drawing rows from the training set *with replacement* until it has as many rows as the original, so some rows appear twice and some not at all. **Bagging** fits one deep tree to each of many bootstrap samples and lets them vote, 1 or 0, with the majority deciding. Leo Breiman's random forests paper of 2001 added a second source of difference: at every split a tree considers only a random subset of the features, which makes the trees less alike still.

afterFigure.text: The trees must differ, because a vote of identical copies is just one tree. If three models were each right 70% of the time and their errors were independent, the majority would be right 3 × 0.7² × 0.3 + 0.7³ = 0.784 of the time, better than any one. Real trees do not err independently, so the gain is smaller, but both resampling and feature subsets exist to push in that direction.

diagram.alt: Two views of a random forest. The first shows three bootstrap samples of six rows, each drawn with replacement, with the rows left out of each listed. The second shows five trees voting 1, 0, 1, 1 and 0, and the forest taking the majority, 1.

reveal.text: The chance of missing the row on one draw is 4 in 5, and the draws are independent.

lead.text: The chance that a given row is missed by a bootstrap sample of n rows is (1 − 1/n)ⁿ, which for n = 20 is 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.36 and which settles at about 0.368 as n grows. Each tree therefore leaves out roughly a third of the rows, called its **out-of-bag** rows, and it never saw them.

afterFigure.text: Scoring each row only with the trees that did not see it gives an honest estimate of the forest's accuracy without setting a validation set aside.

reveal.text: A training score of 1 is what memorisation also produces, so it settles nothing by itself.
Add the probability of exactly two correct, 3 × 0.8² × 0.2, to that of all three correct, 0.8³.

lessons.orientation: Choose a split by Gini impurity and explain why a vote of many different trees beats one deep tree.
lessons.nextAction: Build a single artificial neuron, run a forward pass by hand, and count the parameters in a small network.

blocks.text: A node in a decision tree holds 10 loans, 7 of which were repaid and 3 were not, and the tree has to choose a question that separates them better. Asking whether income is at least 40 thousand sends five loans, all repaid, one way and five loans, two repaid and three not, the other, while asking whether the applicant is under 30 leaves both groups about as mixed as before. A number computed from the counts alone, the drop in Gini impurity, says by how much each question helps: 0.18 for the first and 0.003 for the second.

Choosing the question with the larger drop, again and again, is all a tree needs in order to grow. Grown deep, though, a tree memorises its examples, and the usual repair is a vote among many trees fitted to resampled copies of the data, which is why forests of trees are among the strongest models for tables of data.

diagram.alt: Two views of Gini impurity. The first shows three nodes of ten examples each: all ten positive with Gini 0, seven positive and three negative with Gini 0.42, and five of each with Gini 0.5. The second plots Gini against the share of positives as an arch that is 0 at both ends and 0.5 in the middle.
diagram.caption: Gini impurity for nodes of ten examples. Use the buttons to compare three nodes and then see the whole curve.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute Gini impurity and the gain of a split, and explain why a forest of different trees beats a single deep tree.
intro.whyItMatters: Forests of trees are among the strongest general-purpose models for tables of data.

recap.keyIdea: A tree picks the question that lowers the weighted Gini impurity the most, and a random forest averages many trees grown on resampled data so that their individual quirks are outvoted.

blocks.text: You computed the Gini impurity of a node, weighted the impurity of two children by their sizes, and found the gain, which a tree uses to choose each question. A deep tree memorises, and a vote of trees fitted to bootstrap samples, with features drawn at random at each split, reduces that variance because the trees differ.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to a different family of model, in which a single unit multiplies its inputs by weights, and units are stacked into networks.

lessons.title: Neural networks from one neuron up

lead.text: The straight-line model of the first lesson, ŷ = w·x + b, extends to several inputs by giving each input its own weight, so that **z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b**. A unit that computes this sum and then applies a function f to it, **a = f(z)**, is a **neuron**. Take the weights 1.5 and −1 and the bias −1. With the inputs 3 and 2 the weighted sum is 4.5 − 2 − 1 = 1.5, and with the inputs 2 and 3 it is 3 − 3 − 1 = −1.

afterFigure.text: The weights and the bias are the parameters, and they are learned in the same way as before, by reducing a loss. The new part is the function f, the **activation**.

diagram.alt: A single neuron. Two inputs x1 and x2 are multiplied by the weights 1.5 and minus 1, added to the bias minus 1 to give z, and passed through an activation f. With inputs 3 and 2, z is 1.5, ReLU gives 1.5 and sigmoid gives 0.8176. With inputs 2 and 3, z is minus 1, ReLU gives 0 and sigmoid gives 0.2689.
diagram.caption: One neuron with two inputs. Use the buttons to change the inputs and see z and the two activations.

reveal.text: Multiply each input by its own weight before adding the bias.
The sigmoid is centred on 0, and it maps every z to a value between 0 and 1.

lead.text: The **ReLU**, short for rectified linear unit, is the simplest: **ReLU(z) = max(0, z)**, so a negative z gives 0 and a positive z passes through unchanged. The **sigmoid**, **σ(z) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z))**, squeezes every z into the range between 0 and 1, so that σ(0) = 0.5, σ(1.5) = 0.8176 and σ(−1) = 0.2689, and it is the natural choice for an output that is read as a probability.

afterFigure.text: The two curves are not straight lines, and that is their whole purpose. The sigmoid flattens out for large positive and large negative z, so a very confident neuron changes slowly, and ReLU is flat on one side and straight on the other, which makes it cheap and the usual choice inside a network.

diagram.alt: Two plots of activation functions for z from minus 4 to 4. ReLU is 0 for negative z and equals z for positive z, with marked points at z minus 1 giving 0 and z 1.5 giving 1.5. Sigmoid is an S-shaped curve rising from near 0 to near 1, equal to 0.5 at z 0, with marked points at z minus 1 giving 0.2689 and z 1.5 giving 0.8176.
diagram.caption: ReLU and sigmoid, with the two values of z from the neuron on the earlier screen marked.

lead.text: Putting several neurons side by side gives a **layer**, and feeding one layer's outputs into the next gives a network. In a **fully connected** layer every neuron reads every output of the layer before, so a layer from 3 values to 4 neurons has 3 × 4 = 12 weights, and each of the 4 neurons has one bias, which makes 16 parameters. A second layer from those 4 values to 1 neuron adds 4 × 1 + 1 = 5.

afterFigure.text: The rule is that a layer with n inputs and m neurons has **n × m + m** parameters, and a network's count is the sum over its layers. The 3-4-1 network has 21.

diagram.alt: A fully connected network with 3 inputs, a hidden layer of 4 neurons and 1 output neuron, with a line from every unit to every unit in the next layer. The second view colours the 12 first-layer connections and the 4 second-layer connections and counts the parameters: 3 times 4 plus 4 biases is 16, 4 times 1 plus 1 is 5, 21 in all.
diagram.caption: A 3-4-1 network. Use the buttons to count its parameters.

reveal.text: Count each layer separately: its inputs times its neurons, plus one bias per neuron.

lead.text: Suppose the first layer computes h = 2x + 1 and the second computes y = 3h − 4, with no activation in between. Substituting gives y = 3(2x + 1) − 4 = 6x − 1, which is one straight line with one weight and one bias. However many layers are stacked, the result is a single line, so depth adds nothing at all.

afterFigure.text: Putting a ReLU between the layers changes that. The output becomes y = 3·ReLU(2x + 1) − 4, which is flat at −4 until 2x + 1 reaches 0 at x = −0.5, and then rises along the line. Each bend is built from a neuron, and many neurons together can approximate a curve of almost any shape, which is the source of a network's power.

diagram.alt: The output y of a two-layer network as a function of x. Without an activation between the layers it is the straight line y equals 6x minus 1. With a ReLU between the layers it is flat at minus 4 for x below minus 0.5 and then rises along the same slope.
diagram.caption: Two layers with and without an activation between them. Use the buttons to compare the shape of the output.

reveal.text: Compute h from x first, and then y from h.

lead.text: Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, and for a network the loss depends on a weight only through a chain of layers. Take the chain x → h = w₁·x → ŷ = w₂·h → L = ½(ŷ − 4)², with x = 2, w₁ = 1 and w₂ = 3. The forward pass gives h = 2, ŷ = 6 and L = 2. Going backward, dL/dŷ = ŷ − 4 = 2, and then **dL/dw₂ = dL/dŷ × h = 2 × 2 = 4**.

afterFigure.text: Each earlier gradient reuses the one after it: dL/dh = dL/dŷ × w₂ = 2 × 3 = 6, and **dL/dw₁ = dL/dh × x = 6 × 2 = 12**. This reuse is **backpropagation**, a method for computing the gradients and not a separate way of learning, since the update is still w ← w − η · gradient.

diagram.alt: A small computation graph. The input x is 2 and w1 is 1, giving h equal to 2. Then w2 is 3, giving the prediction y-hat equal to 6, and the loss one half of y-hat minus 4 squared, equal to 2. The second view shows the gradients flowing backward: dL by d y-hat is 2, dL by dw2 is 4, dL by dh is 6 and dL by dw1 is 12.
diagram.caption: The forward pass computes the loss. The backward pass works out how the loss changes with each weight.

steps.headline: Take one gradient step on the chain above, with learning rate η = 0.01 and the gradients dL/dw₂ = 4 and dL/dw₁ = 12.

workedSteps.text: Start with w₂.
The first weight has a much larger gradient, so it moves further.
With the new weights the forward pass gives h = 0.88 × 2 = 1.76 and ŷ = 2.96 × 1.76 = 5.2096.
The loss has fallen from 2 to ½ × (5.2096 − 4)² ≈ 0.73.

steps.headline: Update w₂ for the same chain after a different forward pass: now dL/dw₂ = 8, w₂ = 2 and η = 0.05.

workedSteps.text: The update rule is the same as for any weight, w ← w − η · gradient.
Multiply the learning rate by the gradient.
The weight w₂ is currently 2.

reveal.text: Backpropagation produces each weight's gradient, and gradient descent turns that gradient into a new weight. Neither does the other's job.
Use the same rule for each layer, inputs × neurons + neurons, and add the two layers.

lessons.orientation: Run a forward pass through one neuron and count the parameters of a small fully connected network.
lessons.reviewLabel: Neural networks from one neuron up
lessons.nextAction: Chain the steps of a training run into a pipeline, and record enough about each run to reproduce it.

blocks.text: Two layers that each compute a straight line, h = 2x + 1 and then y = 3h − 4, produce y = 6x − 1, which is one straight line again. Adding a third layer, or a hundredth, gives the same result, so stacking straight lines on their own achieves nothing. Put a ReLU, which replaces every negative number with 0, between the two layers, and the output bends at x = −0.5, flat to the left of that point and rising to the right, and a network builds its curves out of many such bends.
The part that makes the bend is a neuron: a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation such as ReLU.

diagram.alt: The output y of a two-layer network as a function of x. Without an activation between the layers it is the straight line y equals 6x minus 1. With a ReLU between the layers it is flat at minus 4 for x below minus 0.5 and then rises along the same slope.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to run a forward pass through a neuron, count the parameters of a small network, and say what backpropagation computes.
intro.whyItMatters: Neural networks sit behind most of the models you will meet in the next courses.

recap.keyIdea: A neuron applies an activation to a weighted sum, layers of them need that activation to be more than one linear map, and backpropagation delivers the gradients that gradient descent uses.

blocks.text: You computed z = w·x + b for a neuron, applied ReLU and sigmoid to it, counted n × m + m parameters per layer, and saw that layers without an activation collapse to one line. Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards to give each weight its gradient, and the update afterwards is the same gradient descent as before.
