lessons.title: Pipelines and experiment tracking

lead.text: A notebook run on Monday scores 0.81. On Thursday the same notebook, run again after some edits, scores 0.84, and nobody can say whether the rise is real, because the data may have been refreshed, a parameter changed, or a random split fallen differently. The model file from Thursday exists, but nothing says what it was trained on.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is to turn the notebook's steps into a **pipeline**: a script that runs the data, validation, split, features, training and evaluation steps in a fixed order, so that every run follows the same path and each step can write down what it used.

diagram.alt: A row of seven boxes joined by arrows: data, validate, split, features, train, evaluate and register. The first view says one script runs every step in order. The second view lists what each step records: the data hash, a check report, row ids per split, the feature code version, parameters and seed, metrics, and the model with its run id.
diagram.caption: The steps of a training pipeline. Use the buttons to see what each step contributes to the run record.

lead.text: For each run the pipeline writes a **run record**, which has to name the code (the commit identifier), the data (an identifier that changes when the data changes), the parameters, the random seed, the software environment and the resulting metrics.

afterFigure.text: Storing runs in a shared **experiment tracker** makes them comparable: two runs can be set side by side, and the fields that differ are the candidates for any difference in score. The model that comes out of the best run goes into a **model registry** with the identifier of that run attached, so that every model in use can be traced back to how it was made.

reveal.text: Compare the two records field by field and look for the one that changed.

lead.text: Data changes quietly, so naming a file `train.csv` identifies nothing. A **hash** function reads the bytes of the data and produces a short fingerprint: SHA-256 gives 64 hexadecimal characters, the same bytes always give the same fingerprint, and changing a single byte gives a completely different one.

afterFigure.text: The **random seed** fixes the sequence of random numbers, so that splits and initial weights repeat. It is necessary, and it is not enough: a different version of a library may draw numbers in a different order, and some operations on a graphics card run in an order that varies between runs. That is why the environment, with library versions, belongs in the record, and why reproducing a number may mean matching the machine type as well.

reveal.text: Every learning rate is paired with every depth.

lead.text: Tuning settings with cross-validation fits a model for each configuration on each fold, so the number of fits is **configurations × folds**. With 3 learning rates, 4 depths and 5 folds that is 3 × 4 × 5 = 60 fits, and adding a fourth setting with 3 values would multiply it by 3, to 180. A grid grows quickly, which is why the choice of what to tune matters.

afterFigure.text: Once the best configuration is chosen, one further fit on all the training data gives the final model, so the total is 61. The cost is mostly time, and the fits are independent of one another, so they can be run in parallel: 60 fits that take 2 minutes each need 120 minutes one after another, and 30 minutes on 4 machines at once.

reveal.text: Multiply the number of configurations by the number of folds.

steps.headline: Count the fits for 2 learning rates and 3 depths with 4-fold cross-validation, including the final refit.

workedSteps.text: The configurations are every learning rate with every depth.
Multiply by the 4 folds.
The winning configuration is then fitted once more on all the training data.
If each fit takes 3 minutes, the search is 72 minutes before the refit, and the refit adds 3.

steps.headline: Count the fits for 2 optimisers, 3 learning rates and 2 depths with 3-fold cross-validation.

workedSteps.text: The configurations are every combination of the three settings.
Every configuration is fitted again on each of the 3 folds, and no final refit is counted.

lead.text: The Google Cloud guide on continuous delivery and automation of machine learning describes three levels. At level 0 every step is manual: the data scientist runs a notebook, hands over a model file, and an engineer deploys it. At level 1 the training pipeline is automated, so that the model can be retrained on new data by running the pipeline again. At level 2 the pipeline's own code is tested and deployed automatically, which makes changes to it as routine as changes to any other software.

afterFigure.text: A pipeline that retrains on fresh data without a person depends entirely on the checks inside it, the validation of the data and the comparison with the current model, so those checks are where a team builds its confidence.

reveal.text: The seed controls only the random numbers, and other things could differ.
Divide the fits among the workers first, then multiply by the time one fit takes.

lessons.orientation: Say what must be recorded to reproduce a training run and count the fits in a hyperparameter search.

blocks.text: A run record such as commit abc123, data hash 9f2c, learning rate 0.1, depth 4, seed 42 and F1 0.81 says exactly how a score was produced: which version of the code, which bytes of data, which settings and which random choices. With it, a colleague can run the same thing and expect the same number, and when a later run scores 0.84 you can set the two records side by side and see which field changed. Without it, a score is a claim that nobody can check, since the code, the data, the settings, the random split or the software may each have moved.
A pipeline produces such records by running the same steps in the same order every time, with each step writing down what it used.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a run record must hold and count the model fits in a search.
intro.whyItMatters: A result you cannot reproduce is hard to improve and harder to trust.

recap.keyIdea: A pipeline runs the same steps each time, and a run record naming the code, data hash, parameters, seed, environment and metrics makes a result repeatable.

blocks.text: You turned a notebook into pipeline steps, listed the fields a run record needs, and used a hash to identify data by its bytes. A seed helps but does not make a run repeatable on its own, and a grid search costs configurations times folds in fits, with one more for the final model.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the finished model out of the tracker and puts it behind a service, where latency and load decide how it has to be run.

lessons.title: Serving a model and releasing it safely

lead.text: In **batch** serving a job scores every row on a schedule, say every night, and stores the results in a table that other systems read. It suits any case in which the prediction is needed in advance and the inputs are known beforehand, such as a recommendation list for each customer, and it needs no fast service: a job that scores 1.2 million rows at 400 rows per second takes 3,000 seconds, which is 50 minutes.

afterFigure.text: **Online** serving scores each request when it arrives, and it is needed when the input exists only at that moment, such as a card payment to be approved or declined. The trade is between the staleness of batch scores, which can be a day old, and the cost and difficulty of keeping a service fast and available.

diagram.alt: Two ways of serving. In the batch view a nightly job scores every customer ahead of time and stores a table of scores that an application reads later. In the online view a request arrives, a model service scores it immediately, and the score returns within a fraction of a second.
diagram.caption: Scoring ahead of time and scoring on request. Use the buttons to compare the two.

lead.text: A payment check that must answer within 150 milliseconds has to fit the whole request path into that time: the network journey in and out, the lookup of the features the model needs, and the model's own computation.

afterFigure.text: Budgets are usually set on a high **percentile** of latency, such as the 99th, and not on the average, because the slow requests are the ones that users notice and that time out. This makes the model's size a design decision: a larger model may be more accurate offline and still not fit in the time its steps leave.

diagram.alt: A horizontal bar for a 150 millisecond latency budget split into network 30 ms, feature lookup 45 ms and the model 75 ms, which fills the budget exactly. The second view lets the model take 100 ms, so the total is 175 ms and the bar runs 25 ms past the dashed budget line.
diagram.caption: A request's time budget split across its steps. Use the buttons to see what happens when the model is too slow.

reveal.text: Subtract both of the other steps from the budget.
Full capacity leaves nothing spare for a burst or for a replica that fails, which the next screen takes up.

lead.text: A **replica** is one running copy of the service, and capacity is added by running more of them. The number needed is **peak load ÷ (capacity per replica × target utilisation)**, rounded up. For a peak of 900 requests per second and replicas that each handle 60, running at full capacity needs 900 ÷ 60 = 15, while a target of 75% needs 900 ÷ (60 × 0.75) = 20.

afterFigure.text: The extra replicas buy headroom. Waiting time rises sharply as a server nears full utilisation, so a replica run at 100% answers slowly even when it is coping, and a burst of traffic or the loss of a replica pushes the others over. The result is rounded *up*, since a fraction of a replica cannot be run and rounding down would exceed the target.

diagram.alt: Two rows of replica bars. The first view shows 15 replicas each filled to the top, which carries the peak load of 900 requests per second with no spare room. The second view shows 20 replicas each filled to three quarters, carrying the same load with a quarter of each replica spare.
diagram.caption: The same peak load on 15 replicas at full capacity and on 20 replicas at 75%.

steps.headline: Size a service for a peak of 500 requests per second, replicas that each handle 40, and a target utilisation of 70%.

workedSteps.text: Each replica should carry 70% of its capacity at the peak.
Divide the peak load by that usable capacity.
Round up to a whole number of replicas.
At 18 replicas the utilisation at peak is 500 ÷ (18 × 40) ≈ 69%, just under the target.

steps.headline: Size a service for a peak of 1,000 requests per second, replicas that each handle 80, and a target utilisation of 80%.

workedSteps.text: The usable capacity of one replica is 80 × 0.8.
Divide the peak by it.
The result has a fraction, and replicas come in whole numbers.

lead.text: The scores from the test set describe the model on the features as the *training* pipeline computed them. If the serving code computes a feature differently, the model sees values it was not trained on, and the offline score no longer applies. This is **train-serve skew**. A typical cause is two definitions of one feature, for instance an average over 30 days in a SQL query for training and over 7 days in application code for serving, and another is a unit change, such as days in training and hours in serving.

afterFigure.text: The defences are to use one feature definition in both places, as in the second view, and to log the features that serving actually uses so that their distributions can be compared with the training data.

diagram.alt: Two ways of building one feature. In the first view the training pipeline computes the average basket over 30 days in SQL while the serving code computes it over 7 days in Python, so the model sees shifted values. In the second view a single shared feature definition feeds both training and serving.
diagram.caption: Two feature definitions and one shared definition. Use the buttons to compare them.

reveal.text: There are 24 hours in a day.

lead.text: In a **shadow** deployment the candidate receives a copy of live traffic and its answers are logged but never returned, so it can be compared with the current model on real requests without affecting any user. In a **canary** release a small share of requests, such as 5%, is answered by the candidate, while the rest stay on the current model. If the error rate, the latency and the business measure stay within limits, the share is raised in steps up to 100%.

afterFigure.text: The stages are only useful if there is a way back. A **rollback** sends traffic to the previous model again, and it works only if the previous model is still deployed and still compatible with the features and schemas now in place, which is not guaranteed when the new release also changed the features.

diagram.alt: A router splits requests between the current model and a candidate. In shadow mode every request is served by the current model and a copy goes to the candidate, whose answers are only logged. In a canary release 5 percent of requests are served by the candidate. In the full rollout all requests go to the candidate and the current model is kept ready for rollback.

lessons.orientation: Choose batch or online serving, size replicas for a latency target and describe a canary release.
lessons.reviewLabel: Serving a model and releasing it safely
lessons.nextAction: Watch a model after release: compare live feature distributions with training and decide what to monitor when labels arrive late.

blocks.text: A payment check has 150 milliseconds in which to answer, and its path has three steps: the network takes 30, the feature lookup takes 45, and the model has 75. A model that needs 100 makes every request late, however accurate it was on the test set, and that accuracy was in any case measured on features that the serving code may compute differently.

Serving a model is a set of arithmetic and design decisions that sit outside the model, about latency, about how many copies to run at peak, and about how to let a new version meet real traffic without exposing everyone to its faults.

diagram.alt: A horizontal bar for a 150 millisecond latency budget split into network 30 ms, feature lookup 45 ms and the model 75 ms, which fills the budget exactly. The second view lets the model take 100 ms, so the total is 175 ms and the bar runs 25 ms past the dashed budget line.
diagram.caption: A request's time budget split across its steps. Use the buttons to see what happens when the model is too slow.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between batch and online serving, size replicas for a peak, and describe a staged release.
intro.whyItMatters: These decisions decide whether a good model can be used at all.

recap.keyIdea: Serving is chosen by when the answer is needed, latency and replicas follow from the budget and the peak load, and a staged release limits how far a fault can spread.

blocks.text: You chose between scoring ahead of time and scoring on request, split a latency budget across a request path, and sized replicas as peak load ÷ (capacity × target utilisation), rounded up. A model is released through shadow and canary stages, with a rollback that is only as good as the compatibility of the old model with the current features.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what happens after release, when live data slowly stops resembling the data the model was trained on.

lessons.title: Monitoring and drift

lead.text: Suppose the order value of customers was cut at its quartiles when the model was trained, so that each of four bins held 25% of the orders. A week later the bins hold 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%, because orders have become smaller, and the model, which has never seen so many small orders, goes on answering without any sign of strain. A change in the distribution of the inputs is called **data drift**.

afterFigure.text: The service stays up, latency stays flat and predictions keep coming out, so it has to be looked for with a measure.

reveal.text: A measure of change should say that nothing has changed when the two distributions agree.

lead.text: For each bin let e be the expected share, from training, and a the actual share, from live data. The **population stability index** is **PSI = Σ (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e)**, summed over the bins. Each term is zero when a = e, and positive when a differs from e in either direction, because (a − e) and ln(a ÷ e) always have the same sign. The index is therefore never negative, and a larger value means a larger shift.

afterFigure.text: For the four bins above the terms are 0.0705, 0.0091, 0.0112 and 0.1374, which add up to a PSI of 0.228. The last term dominates, since the highest bin has lost more than half of its share, from 25% to 10%. Looking at the terms says *where* the shift is, and not only how large it is, which is the useful part for finding the cause.

reveal.text: Work out the term for each bin separately, then add them.

lead.text: The values that are quoted are that a PSI below 0.1 means little change, from 0.1 to 0.25 a moderate change worth a look, and above 0.25 a large one. These are conventions from credit-risk practice and not laws: no theorem puts the boundary at 0.25, and a feature can have a large PSI and little effect on the model, or a small PSI and a large one.

afterFigure.text: The number of bins and their width also matter, since the same data gives different PSI values under different binning, which is why the bins are fixed once from the training data and reused. The PSI says that a distribution has moved. It does not say that predictions have worsened, which only labels can show.

workedSteps.text: The first bin has moved down by 0.1, from 0.4 to 0.3.
The second bin stays at 0.4.
The third bin has moved up by 0.1, from 0.2 to 0.3.
Add the three terms.

steps.headline: Work out the PSI for two bins with expected shares 0.5 and 0.5 and actual shares 0.3 and 0.7.

workedSteps.text: The first bin has fallen from 0.5 to 0.3.
The second bin has risen from 0.5 to 0.7.
The PSI is the sum of the two bin terms.

steps.headline: Data drift, concept drift and delay

lead.text: **Data drift** is a change in the inputs, and the PSI measures it. **Concept drift** is a change in what the inputs mean for the label: customers change what they buy, so the same features now imply a different outcome, and the model's rule is out of date while the inputs look exactly as before. A PSI on the inputs cannot see it, and only the labels can, by showing the accuracy fall.

afterFigure.text: The labels may be slow to arrive. A fraud label arrives when a chargeback does, a default label arrives months after a loan, and with a **label delay** of 30 days the accuracy of today's predictions cannot be computed until next month. Input drift tends to appear first for that reason, and 'accuracy is stable' may only mean that the accuracy of old predictions is stable.

diagram.alt: Three kinds of change after release. In data drift the distribution of an input shifts while its relationship to the label holds. In concept drift the inputs look the same while the relationship to the label changes, shown by a flatter line against the original dashed one. In label delay a prediction on day 0 is scored only when its label arrives on day 30.
diagram.caption: Data drift, concept drift and label delay compared. Use the buttons to see each.

reveal.text: Ask whether the input distribution changed, the relationship to the label changed, or both.

lead.text: Three kinds of signal are available straight away. The **input distributions** of each feature, tracked with a measure such as the PSI each day, show data drift. The **prediction distribution**, such as the share of rows flagged positive, shows how the model's behaviour has changed. **Data quality** checks, such as the share of missing values and the range of each feature, catch a broken upstream feed, which is the commonest cause of a sudden shift.

afterFigure.text: Business outcomes that arrive faster than the label, such as the rate of customer complaints or manual review overturns, act as proxies. When the labels do arrive they are matched back to the predictions, and the accuracy is computed for the period they cover.

diagram.alt: Two line charts of illustrative data over 30 days. The daily population stability index of one feature stays below 0.1 until about day 18, passes 0.1, and passes 0.25 by about day 26. The share of predictions that are positive rises from about 5 percent to about 8 percent over the last 15 days.
diagram.caption: What can be watched while labels are late. The data are illustrative, and the lines mark the conventional PSI levels 0.1 and 0.25.

reveal.text: A prediction made on day d has its label on day d + 30.
Work out one term per bin, (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e), and add them.

lessons.orientation: Compute a population stability index and decide what to monitor when labels arrive late.
lessons.nextAction: Compare a model's results across groups, write a model card, and place the work under the four NIST AI RMF functions.

blocks.text: The order value of customers was cut into four bins at training time, each holding 25% of the orders. One week after release the same bins hold 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%. The service is up, latency is flat and every request returns an answer, and yet the model is being asked about a population that has shifted towards small orders, which it saw less often in training than it now sees them.

None of the usual health checks reports a shift like this, because nothing has failed, so it has to be measured against the distribution the model learned from. Labels that would show a fall in accuracy often arrive a month late, which means the measures that work today are the ones on inputs and predictions, and with them you can see **drift** weeks before the accuracy figures catch up.

intro.whyItMatters: Models degrade quietly, and the only defence is a measure you chose in advance.

recap.keyIdea: The PSI sums how far each bin's live share has moved from its training share, and while labels are late the inputs, the predictions and data quality are what can be watched.

blocks.text: You computed the PSI as the sum of (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e) over the bins, found that it is zero when nothing has shifted, and that the usual 0.1 and 0.25 levels are conventions. Data drift moves the inputs, concept drift moves their meaning, and label delay means accuracy lags both.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson asks a different kind of question about a model in use: whether it works as well for every group of people it affects, and how that is recorded.

lessons.title: Fairness, documentation and risk

lead.text: A lender's model approves 60 of 120 applicants in group X and 30 of 100 in group Y. The share of a group that receives the positive decision is its **selection rate**, which is 0.50 for X and 0.30 for Y. Asking for the same selection rate in every group is called **demographic parity**, and here the groups are 0.20 apart. Whether that gap is a fault depends on the situation, and the first step is to measure it, which an overall accuracy never does.

afterFigure.text: Selection rate ignores who actually deserved the decision. Of the 80 creditworthy applicants in group X, the model approved 52, and of the 50 in group Y it approved 25, so the share of qualified people who are found is 52 ÷ 80 = 0.65 for X and 25 ÷ 50 = 0.50 for Y. This is the **true positive rate**, the recall of the earlier lessons, and comparing it between groups is called **equal opportunity**. The gap is 0.15, a different gap from the 0.20 above.

diagram.alt: A table of counts for two groups. Group X has 120 applicants, of whom 80 are qualified, and 60 were selected, 52 of them creditworthy. Group Y has 100 applicants, 50 creditworthy, 30 selected and 25 of those creditworthy. The second view adds the selection rates, 0.50 and 0.30, and the true positive rates, 0.65 and 0.50.

reveal.text: Work out each group's rate as selected divided by applicants, then subtract.
Parity in one measure says nothing about the other, since the two measures divide by different counts.

lead.text: The protected attribute that defines the groups, such as gender, can be left out of the features, and its effect usually remains. A postcode, a first name or a pattern of purchases can be correlated with the attribute, so the model recovers it from them, and the bias in the labels it learned from comes through. The remedy is to keep the attribute available for *auditing*, so that the metrics can still be computed per group, even if the model is not given it.

afterFigure.text: The measures also conflict. When the groups have different base rates, a classifier can in general not equalise selection rates, true positive rates and precision at the same time, apart from special cases such as a perfect classifier, so a choice has to be made. The choice depends on what each kind of error costs the people affected, and it is a decision for the owners of the system and not a quantity that the data settles.

reveal.text: Think about what other columns might carry information about the removed one.

lead.text: Margaret Mitchell and colleagues proposed in 2019 that every released model should come with a short document, a **model card**, with nine sections.

afterFigure.text: The most useful entries are the plain limits. A card for a loan-ranking model says that it is meant to order applications for an officer to review and that automatic rejection is out of scope, it names the data it was evaluated on, and it reports the selection rate and true positive rate per group.

diagram.alt: A model card drawn as a page. The first view lists its nine sections: model details, intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, training data, quantitative analyses, ethical considerations, and caveats and recommendations. The second view fills four of them for a loan-ranking model: intended use, out of scope, evaluation data and metrics.

reveal.text: It was proposed by Mitchell and colleagues in 2019, and it works like a data sheet for a model.

lead.text: NIST published version 1.0 of its Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework in January 2023, as a voluntary framework. Its core has four functions. **Govern** sets the policies, roles and culture that make risk work happen, and it runs across the other three. **Map** establishes the context and identifies the risks, **Measure** analyses and tracks them with metrics, and **Manage** prioritises the risks and acts on them.

afterFigure.text: The functions work as a way to sort the tasks of a project and to see what is missing. Writing a model's intended use belongs to Map, computing the per-group rates belongs to Measure, rolling back a failing release belongs to Manage, and naming an owner for each release belongs to Govern.

diagram.alt: The four functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Govern is a bar across the top, covering the rest. Below it, Map, Measure and Manage follow one another. The second view maps four tasks to functions: writing intended use to Map, computing per-group true positive rate to Measure, rolling back a failing model to Manage, and assigning an owner to Govern.

Computing a rate for each group is the second task.

workedSteps.math: roll back a failing release: Manage

workedSteps.text: Naming an owner is a matter of roles and accountability, which cuts across the other three.

reveal.text: Describing the system, its data and its limits sets the context in which risks arise, which is the work of Map.
Work out each group's rate as creditworthy applicants approved divided by creditworthy applicants.

lessons.orientation: Compare a metric across groups, write what a model card must say, and place work under the four NIST AI RMF functions.
lessons.nextAction: You can now fit and evaluate a model honestly, ship it, watch it, and say who it serves and how well.

blocks.text: A lender's model approves 60 of the 120 applicants in group X and 30 of the 100 in group Y, which is a selection rate of 0.50 against 0.30. Of the people who deserved a loan, it finds 52 of 80 in group X and 25 of 50 in group Y, a rate of 0.65 against 0.50. An accuracy figure for the two groups together contains neither gap.

Computing the metrics for each group is how such gaps become visible, and a written record of what a model is for, what it was built from and how it performs for each group keeps them visible to the people who decide whether the model should be used. Those measurements do not settle what is fair, which is a question for the people who own the system, but they give that decision facts to rest on.

Group Y has 100 applicants, 50 creditworthy, 30 selected and 25 of those creditworthy. The second view adds the selection rates, 0.50 and 0.30, and the true positive rates, 0.65 and 0.50.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compare selection rate and true positive rate across groups, say what a model card holds, and place tasks under Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
intro.whyItMatters: A model that works on average can still fail the people it affects, and this lesson shows how to check.

recap.keyIdea: Per-group metrics show gaps that one overall number hides, a model card records a model's purpose and limits, and the NIST AI RMF sorts the risk work into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.

blocks.text: You computed selection rate and true positive rate for two groups and found that equal selection does not guarantee equal true positive rates, and that removing a protected attribute leaves its proxies behind. A model card keeps a model's intended use, data and per-group results together, and the four functions of the NIST AI RMF place that work within an organisation.

questions.prompt: The rule is ŷ = x. A student studied 4 hours and scored 6 marks. What is the residual, label minus prediction?
hints: The prediction is ŷ = 4.
The residual is the label minus the prediction.
Compute 6 − 4.
questions.onCorrect: The residual is positive, so the rule predicts too low for this student.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts in the wrong order. The residual is the label minus the prediction.

questions.prompt: The rule is ŷ = x + 1. For the examples (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 3) and (4, 6), what is the sum of the squared residuals?
hints: Find the prediction ŷ = x + 1 for each x first.
Subtract each prediction from its label to get four residuals.
Square each residual, then add.
questions.onCorrect: Shifting the line helped, but the slope still needs changing to reach the minimum of 1.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the residuals −1 + 0 − 1 + 1 without squaring them, so the signs cancel.
The residuals are not all zero. Square each one before adding.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Predictions 2, 3, 4, 5 give residuals −1, 0, −1, 1, and the squares 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 add to 3.

questions.prompt: On the examples (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 3) and (4, 6), the rule ŷ = x has a sum of squared residuals of 5, and the best line has 1.5. The rule is moved up by 1, to ŷ = x + 1. Roughly where will its sum of squared residuals fall?
hints: Look at the signs of the residuals of ŷ = x on the four examples: is the line above or below them?
Moving the line up changes its height but not its slope.

acceptedIdeas: Between 1.5 and 5, because it fits better than ŷ = x but cannot beat the best line
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Between 1.5 and 5, because it fits better than ŷ = x but cannot beat the best line

questions.onCorrect: The residuals become −1, 0, −1 and 1, and their squares add to 3. Shifting the line helped, but reaching 1.5 also needs a change of slope.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule ŷ = x has residuals 0, 1, 0 and 2, so it sits on or below every example, and raising it brings it closer to most of them. The sum comes out at 3, which is lower than 5.
The best line, ŷ = 1.5x − 0.5, has a different slope from ŷ = x + 1, and sliding a line up or down cannot change its slope. The shifted rule has a sum of 3, which is still above 1.5.
The best line is the one with the smallest sum of squared residuals, so no other rule can have a smaller sum. The shifted rule comes out at 3.

choices.label: Above 5, because moving a line away from where it was always makes it worse
Exactly 1.5, because moving the line up makes it the best line
Below 1.5, because the shifted line would fit better than the best line
Between 1.5 and 5, because it fits better than ŷ = x but cannot beat the best line

questions.prompt: For the examples (1, 3), (2, 5) and (3, 10), with x̄ = 2 and ȳ = 6, what is Sxy?
hints: Multiply each pair of distances: (x − x̄) with (y − ȳ).
The products are (−1)(−3), (0)(−1) and (1)(4).
Add 3, 0 and 4.
questions.onCorrect: With Sxx = 2 this gives w = 3.5, and b = 6 − 3.5 × 2 = −1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the slope w, which is Sxy divided by Sxx. Sxy is the sum before dividing.

questions.prompt: The fitted rule is ŷ = 3.5x − 1. What does it predict for a student who studied 4 hours?
hints: Replace x with 4.
Multiply 3.5 by 4 first.
Then subtract 1.
questions.onCorrect: The prediction 13 lies beyond the largest example, a stretch of the line that no example has checked.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the intercept b = −1.

questions.prompt: After fitting, the four examples are deleted and only w = 1.5 and b = −0.5 are kept. What can the model still do?
hints: Ask what the formula ŷ = 1.5x − 0.5 needs as input.
questions.onCorrect: The two parameters define the whole line, so any hours value gives a prediction, with no look-up of examples.

misconceptions.feedback: The residuals show that the line does not reproduce the marks: the third student's 3 comes back as 4. The examples are not recoverable from two numbers.
The formula accepts any x. It is not a table of the four hours.

choices.label: Predict a mark for any number of hours, such as 5.
Recover each of the four original marks exactly.
Predict only for the four hours it was fitted on.

acceptedIdeas: Predict a mark for any number of hours, such as 5.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Predict a mark for any number of hours, such as 5.

questions.prompt: Fit y = w·x + b to the points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5) and (4, 8), which have x̄ = 2.5 and ȳ = 4.75. What is w?
hints: Sxy adds (x − x̄)(y − ȳ) over the four points.
Sxy is 9.5 and Sxx is 5.
w is Sxy divided by Sxx.
questions.onCorrect: With w = 1.9, b = 4.75 − 1.9 × 2.5 = 0, so the line passes through the origin.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Sxy. The slope also divides by Sxx.
That is the first label divided by the first input, which uses one point. The fit uses all four.

questions.prompt: The fitted line for those points is ŷ = 1.9x, with b = 0. What does the model predict for x = 5?
hints: Replace x with 5.
Multiply 1.9 by 5.
Add b, which is 0.
questions.onCorrect: The prediction is 9.5 and lies beyond the largest example, x = 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the label of the last example, not the model's prediction.
That evaluates the line at 4. The new input is 5.

questions.prompt: The line ŷ = 1.9x gives residuals 0.1, 0.2, −0.7 and 0.4 on the four points. What is its mean squared error?
hints: Square each residual.
The squares are 0.01, 0.04, 0.49 and 0.16.
Add them and divide by 4.
questions.onCorrect: The sum of squares is 0.70 and dividing by the four examples gives the mean.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of squares. The mean divides by the number of examples.
The residuals do not cancel once squared: squares are all positive.

questions.prompt: Why does the formula b = ȳ − w·x̄ place the line where it does?
hints: Put x = x̄ into ŷ = w·x + b and see what comes out.
questions.onCorrect: Substituting x̄ gives ŷ = w·x̄ + ȳ − w·x̄ = ȳ, so the fitted line always passes through the means.

misconceptions.feedback: The intercept is b = −0.5 here, so the line does not pass through the origin in general.
The residuals here are 0, 0.5, −1 and 0.5. A line cannot pass through every point.

choices.label: It makes the line pass through (x̄, ȳ), the centre of the examples
It makes the line pass through the origin, where x and y are both zero
It makes every residual equal to zero, so the line fits all four points

acceptedIdeas: It makes the line pass through (x̄, ȳ), the centre of the examples
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It makes the line pass through (x̄, ȳ), the centre of the examples

questions.prompt: On the examples (1, 1) and (2, 3), what is the gradient Σ xᵢ(w·xᵢ − yᵢ) at w = 2?
hints: Replace w with 2 in each residual w·x − y.
Weight each residual by its own x before adding.
The first residual is for x = 1 and the second for x = 2.
questions.onCorrect: A positive gradient puts w = 2 right of the minimum at 1.4, so the update will lower w.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the residuals without weighting the second by its x = 2.
The sign is reversed. At w = 2 the predictions are above the labels, so the slope is positive.

questions.prompt: Why does the update subtract the gradient from w?
hints: Ask which direction the gradient points, uphill or downhill.
questions.onCorrect: The gradient points in the direction of increasing loss, so subtracting it moves w towards lower loss.

misconceptions.feedback: The gradient points away from the minimum, uphill, so the minus sign is what sends w towards it.
The gradient is negative at w = 0 but positive at w = 2, so its sign depends on the position.

choices.label: The gradient is always negative, so subtracting makes w larger.
The gradient points uphill, so moving against it lowers the loss.
The gradient points towards the minimum, so adding it would overshoot.

acceptedIdeas: The gradient points uphill, so moving against it lowers the loss.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gradient points uphill, so moving against it lowers the loss.

questions.prompt: Start at w = 3 with gradient 8 and learning rate η = 0.1. What is w after one update?
hints: The update is w ← w − η · gradient.
Multiply 0.1 by 8 first.
Subtract that product from 3.
questions.onCorrect: The gradient is positive, so the step lowers w, from 3 to 2.2, towards the minimum at 1.4.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds η times the gradient. The update subtracts it.
That is the step size alone. The new w is the old w minus that step.

questions.prompt: From w = 0 with gradient −7, apply the update once with η = 0.4. What is w?
hints: The update is w ← w − η · gradient.
Multiply 0.4 by −7.

The folds are cut once and each is held out in turn, so every row belongs to exactly one held-out fold and is scored in that round.

choices.label: It depends on the random split, so some rows may never be scored
Four times
Five times
Exactly once

questions.prompt: A data set of 1,800 rows is split into 6 folds. How many rows does each model train on?
hints: Each fold holds 1,800 ÷ 6 rows.
Training uses every fold except one.
Subtract one fold from 1,800.
questions.onCorrect: Each model trains on five folds of 300 rows and scores on the sixth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one fold, the part used for scoring.
That is every row. One fold is held out each round.

questions.prompt: Two settings both average 0.78 across folds, and one has a much smaller spread. Why prefer it?
hints: The means are the same, so the difference lies in the spread.
questions.onCorrect: A small spread means the score hardly depends on which rows were held out, so it is more predictable on new rows.

misconceptions.feedback: The two means are equal, so the spread cannot be a difference in the average. It tells how much the score moves from fold to fold.
Spread says nothing about flexibility. It measures how much the fold scores vary.

choices.label: A smaller spread means the model is more flexible.
A smaller spread means a higher average score on new data
Its score is more predictable on new data.

acceptedIdeas: Its score is more predictable on new data.

questions.prompt: Setting B's fold scores have a sum of squared deviations of 0.0176 over 5 folds. What is the standard deviation, to three decimal places?
hints: Divide the sum of squares by k − 1.
The variance is 0.0176 ÷ 4.
Take the square root of the variance.
questions.onCorrect: B's standard deviation is about four times A's 0.016, though the two means are equal.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by k = 5 and not k − 1 = 4.

questions.prompt: A model has a training error far below its validation error. Which change is most likely to reduce the gap?
hints: The gap means the model has high variance.
questions.onCorrect: A stronger penalty restrains the parameters, which lowers variance and narrows the gap at the cost of some training fit.

misconceptions.feedback: A weaker penalty makes the model more flexible and would widen the gap.
Removing the validation set hides the gap and does nothing to the model.

choices.label: Remove the validation set.
Raise the penalty strength λ.
Lower the penalty strength λ.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Raise the penalty strength λ.

questions.prompt: A model has parameters w₁ = 3 and w₂ = −4, a mean squared error of 1.0 and λ = 0.1. What is MSE + λ·(w₁² + w₂²)?
hints: Square each parameter separately.
Add the squares.
Multiply by λ and add the mean squared error.
questions.onCorrect: The penalty is 2.5, because 25 is large, and a model with many large parameters pays for all of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the penalty as λ·(3 − 4)², which is not the sum of squares.
That is the penalty alone, without the mean squared error.

questions.prompt: The mean squared error is 3, the parameter is w = 2 and λ = 0.5. What is the L2 penalised loss, MSE + λ·w²?
hints: Square w.
Multiply the square by λ.
Add the result to the mean squared error.
questions.onCorrect: The penalty adds 2 to the error of 3, and the L1 version of the same loss would be 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses |w|, the L1 penalty, instead of w².
That is the mean squared error alone, without the penalty.

questions.prompt: Five folds score 0.82, 0.80, 0.85, 0.78 and 0.80. What is the mean?
hints: Add the five scores.
The sum is 4.05.
Divide the sum by 5.
questions.onCorrect: The mean of 0.81 is the cross-validation estimate for this setting.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle fold score, the median, not the mean.
That is the sum. The mean divides it by 5.

questions.prompt: With 1,000 rows and 5-fold cross-validation, how many rows train each model?
hints: Each fold holds 1,000 ÷ 5 rows.
Training uses every fold except the held-out one.
Subtract one fold from 1,000.
questions.onCorrect: Each model trains on four folds of 200 rows and scores on the remaining fold of 200.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one fold, the part held out for scoring.
That is every row. One fold is held out in each round.

questions.prompt: A column has the values 4, 8, 12 and 20. What is the min-max scaled value of 12?
hints: The smallest value is 4 and the largest is 20.
The numerator is 12 − 4 and the denominator is 20 − 4.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: 12 sits halfway between 4 and 20, so it scales to 0.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 12 by 20 and ignores the minimum. Subtract the minimum first.
That is the numerator alone. Divide by the range, 20 − 4.

questions.prompt: What is the median of the values 2, 3, 5, 6 and 84?
hints: Put the values in order.
The median is the middle one of five.
It is the third value.
questions.onCorrect: The median is 5, unmoved by the 84, whereas the mean is 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 84 pulls up.
That is the fourth value. The middle of five is the third.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In order 2, 3, 5, 6, 84, the third value is 5.

questions.prompt: A column of incomes, in thousands, holds 2, 3, 5, 6 and 84, and one entry in another row is missing and has to be filled in. Which stand-in is closest to what a typical row in the column looks like?
hints: Four of the five values are small, and one is very large.

acceptedIdeas: The middle value once the five are put in order
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The middle value once the five are put in order

questions.onCorrect: The middle value, the median, is 5, and the 84 does not move it, while the mean is 20.

misconceptions.feedback: The single 84 pulls the mean up to 20, a figure none of the other four values comes near.
The 84 is the one value unlike the others, so filling the gap with it makes the row look like the outlier.

choices.label: The largest value, 84, because it is the biggest seen
The mean, the sum of the five values divided by five
The middle value once the five are put in order

questions.prompt: A column with 12 distinct levels is one-hot encoded. How many columns does it become?
hints: Each level gets its own column.
There is no separate column for the whole feature.
Count the levels.
questions.onCorrect: Each row has exactly one 1 among the 12 columns, and the other 11 are 0.

misconceptions.feedback: Dropping one level is possible in some models, but plain one-hot encoding keeps every level.
That is the number of 1s in each row. The number of columns is the number of levels.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One column per level gives 12 columns.

questions.prompt: A model predicts whether customers will cancel next month, using the columns `months`, `plan`, `support_calls_last_30_days` and `cancellation_reason`. Which column leaks the label?
hints: Which column could only be filled in after a customer has cancelled?

questions.onCorrect: The reason is recorded at cancellation, so it exists only for customers whose outcome is already known.

misconceptions.feedback: The number of months is known before any cancellation, so it can legitimately be used.

choices.label: `cancellation_reason`
`months`
`support_calls_last_30_days`
`plan`

questions.prompt: Why is a result outside 0 to 1 acceptable for the scaled test value?
hints: The scaler's minimum and maximum come from the training rows.
questions.onCorrect: A value beyond the training range scales beyond 0 to 1, which is honest information about how unlike the training rows it is.

misconceptions.feedback: The fit is correct. The leaky alternative would hide the difference by letting the test row set the maximum.

choices.label: The scaler was fitted on the training rows only, and the test value is above all of them
The scaler was fitted incorrectly, so the test value should have been scaled again
Min-max scaling is defined so that every value, new or old, ends up between 0 and 1

acceptedIdeas: The scaler was fitted on the training rows only, and the test value is above all of them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The scaler was fitted on the training rows only, and the test value is above all of them

questions.prompt: With training mean 5 and standard deviation 2, what is the standardised value of 11?
hints: The formula is z = (x − μ) ÷ σ.
The numerator is 11 − 5.
Divide it by 2.
questions.onCorrect: A z of 3 means the test value is three standard deviations above the training mean, which is unusual for these training rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the numerator alone. Divide by σ = 2.
That divides 11 − 5 by 4, the variance, and not by σ.

questions.prompt: A scaler is fitted to all 1,000 rows, and 20% of the rows are then held out as the test set. How many test rows influenced the scaler?
hints: The scaler was fitted before the split.
It therefore used every row.
How many of the 1,000 rows end up in the test set?
questions.onCorrect: All 200 test rows shaped the scaler, so the test score is slightly optimistic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the correct answer if the scaler were fitted after the split, on the 800 training rows only.
That is the number of training rows. The question asks about test rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The scaler used all 1,000 rows, which include the 200 that later became the test set.

questions.prompt: The values are 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. What is the min-max scaled value of 20?
hints: The smallest value is 10 and the largest is 50.
Subtract the minimum from 20, and from 50.
Divide the first difference by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The scaled values are 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1, evenly spaced as the originals were.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 20 by 50 and ignores the minimum.
That is the numerator alone. Divide by the range, 50 − 10.

questions.prompt: The values 4, 6, 10 and 100 have a missing entry in another row, to be filled with the median. What value is used?
hints: Put the values in order, and note that there are four of them.
With an even count, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
Those two are 6 and 10.
questions.onCorrect: The median is 8, whereas the mean, 30, is pulled up by the 100.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 100 pulls up.
That is the third value only. With four values, average the middle two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The middle values are 6 and 10, and (6 + 10) ÷ 2 = 8.

questions.prompt: A model predicts hospital readmission using a column that is filled in at the discharge review, after the outcome is known. What is this problem called?
hints: Ask whether the column exists at the moment the prediction would be made.
questions.onCorrect: A column recorded after the outcome carries the answer into the features, so the model's score is not a fair estimate.

misconceptions.feedback: Class imbalance concerns how rare the positive class is, not when a column is recorded.
Underfitting is a model too simple to fit the data. This model may fit very well, for the wrong reason.
Covariate shift is a change in inputs between training and use, and it does not describe a column that contains the outcome.

choices.label: Underfitting
Class imbalance
Target leakage
Covariate shift

acceptedIdeas: Target leakage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Target leakage

questions.prompt: A node has 9 positive and 1 negative example. What is its Gini impurity?
hints: The shares are 0.9 and 0.1.
Square each share and add the squares.
Subtract that sum from 1.
questions.onCorrect: The node is nearly pure, so its impurity of 0.18 is well below the 0.5 of an even mix.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the squared shares. Gini is 1 minus that sum.
That is 0.9 × 0.1. Gini is 1 − 0.9² − 0.1², which is twice that product.

questions.prompt: Five examples go to a child with Gini 0 and five go to a child with Gini 0.48. What is the weighted child impurity?
hints: Each child has half of the examples.
Multiply each child's Gini by its share.
Add the two products.
questions.onCorrect: The pure child adds nothing, so the weighted impurity is half the other child's, 0.24.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the impure child's Gini alone, without its weight of one half.
That averages the two children's sizes and not their impurities.

questions.prompt: The node of 7 repaid and 3 unpaid loans has a Gini impurity of 0.42. A question sends 5 loans to one child, all repaid, with a Gini of 0, and 5 to the other, 2 repaid and 3 not, with a Gini of 0.48. Taking each child in proportion to its size, how mixed are the two children together compared with the parent?
hints: Each child holds half the loans, so each counts for half.
Half of 0 plus half of 0.48 is the combined figure.

acceptedIdeas: Clearly less mixed, roughly half the parent's impurity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Clearly less mixed, roughly half the parent's impurity

questions.onCorrect: The combined impurity is 0.5 × 0 + 0.5 × 0.48 = 0.24, so the question lowers the impurity by 0.18.

misconceptions.feedback: The 0.48 belongs to only half the loans, and the other half sit in a pure child with impurity 0, so the two together are much less mixed than the parent.
Half the loans now sit in a pure child, which counts for a great deal: the combined impurity is 0.5 × 0 + 0.5 × 0.48 = 0.24, well below 0.42.

choices.label: More mixed than the parent, because 0.48 is above 0.42
About as mixed as the parent
Clearly less mixed, roughly half the parent's impurity

questions.prompt: Why is each child's Gini multiplied by its share of the examples?
hints: Imagine a split with one tiny, impure child and one large, pure child.
questions.onCorrect: Weighting by size makes the total reflect how many examples end up in an impure node, so a tiny impure child hardly matters.

misconceptions.feedback: The weighted sum of values below 0.5 is below 0.5 already. Weighting is there for fairness between children of different sizes.
Pure children are not ignored. They contribute 0 because their Gini is 0.

choices.label: So that pure children are ignored.
So that a large child counts for more than a small one.
So that the result is always between 0 and 1.

acceptedIdeas: So that a large child counts for more than a small one.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: So that a large child counts for more than a small one.

questions.prompt: The parent has Gini 0.42 and the weighted child impurity of the loan-term split is 0.4. What is the gain, to three decimal places?
hints: The gain is the parent's impurity minus the weighted child impurity.
Subtract 0.4 from 0.42.
The result is small.
questions.onCorrect: The loan-term question barely reduces impurity, so the tree would choose income, whose gain is 0.18, over it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weighted child impurity. The gain is the parent's impurity minus it.
That is the gain of the income split, not the loan-term split.

questions.prompt: A bootstrap sample draws 5 times, with replacement, from 5 rows. What is the probability that a particular row is never drawn, to three decimal places?
hints: On one draw the row is missed with probability 4/5.
The five draws are independent.
Multiply 0.8 by itself five times.
questions.onCorrect: About a third of the rows are left out of each bootstrap sample, and that fraction tends to 0.368 as the number of rows grows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the probability of being drawn on one draw. The question needs five missed draws in a row.
That is the chance of being missed once. All five draws must miss.

questions.prompt: A tree with unlimited depth has a training accuracy of 1.0. What does that suggest about its validation accuracy?
hints: Compare the degree-9 polynomial of the generalisation lesson.
questions.onCorrect: A tree that fits every training example, noise included, usually does worse on new rows, which is the high variance that bagging averages away.

misconceptions.feedback: A perfect training score does not carry over to new rows. A tree can reach it by memorising.
The validation score is measured on rows the tree never saw, and it is typically lower.

choices.label: It will also be 1.0, because the tree is perfect.
It will probably be lower, because the tree has memorised noise.
It will be exactly the same as the training accuracy.

acceptedIdeas: It will probably be lower, because the tree has memorised noise.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It will probably be lower, because the tree has memorised noise.

questions.prompt: Three models are each correct with probability 0.8, independently, and a majority vote decides. What is the probability that the vote is correct?
hints: The vote is right when two or three models are right.
Exactly two right: choose which two, 3 × 0.8² × 0.2.
Add the probability that all three are right, 0.8³.
questions.onCorrect: The vote beats each single model's 0.8 only because their errors are assumed independent, and trees fitted to similar data are not fully independent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the accuracy of one model. The vote is more accurate when errors are independent.
That is exactly two correct. The probability of all three correct, 0.512, is also a win.

questions.prompt: A node has 6 positive and 4 negative examples. What is its Gini impurity?
hints: The class shares are 0.6 and 0.4.
Square each share and add the squares.
Subtract that sum from 1.
questions.onCorrect: The node is fairly mixed, close to the 0.5 of an even split.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the squared shares. Gini is 1 minus that sum.
That is 0.6 × 0.4. Gini is 1 − 0.6² − 0.4², which is twice that product.

questions.prompt: The node is split into a left child of 4 positive and 1 negative (Gini 0.32) and a right child of 2 positive and 3 negative (Gini 0.48). What is the weighted child Gini?
hints: Each child holds 5 of the 10 examples.
Weight each Gini by one half.
questions.onCorrect: The weighted impurity of 0.40 is below the parent's 0.48.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two Ginis without the weights.
That is the parent's impurity and the right child's, not the weighted average.

questions.prompt: What is the impurity decrease, the gain, of that split?
hints: The parent's Gini was 0.48.
The weighted child Gini was 0.40.
Subtract the second from the first.
questions.onCorrect: A gain of 0.08 is modest, so another question might do better.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weighted child impurity. The gain is the difference from the parent's.
That adds the two values. The gain subtracts the child impurity from the parent's.

questions.prompt: A neuron has weights 1.5 and −1 and bias −1. What is z for the inputs x₁ = 1 and x₂ = 4?
hints: Multiply 1.5 by 1, and −1 by 4.
Add the two products.
Then add the bias, −1.
questions.onCorrect: A negative z gives 0 after ReLU, so this neuron is silent for these inputs.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the bias of −1.
That has the wrong sign. The second weight is −1, so its term is −4.

questions.prompt: The sigmoid is σ(z) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z)). What is σ(0)?
hints: e^0 equals 1.
The denominator is 1 + 1.
Take 1 divided by that.
questions.onCorrect: The sigmoid is centred at 0.5, and it rises towards 1 for positive z and falls towards 0 for negative z.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the limit for a very large positive z. At z = 0 the denominator is 2.
That is the limit for a very negative z. At z = 0 the output is in the middle.

questions.prompt: The sigmoid activation is σ(z) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z)), and its output always lies between 0 and 1. Where does a sigmoid neuron's output sit when its weighted sum is z = 0?
hints: Any number raised to the power 0 is 1.

acceptedIdeas: Exactly halfway between 0 and 1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Exactly halfway between 0 and 1

misconceptions.feedback: At z = 0 the term e^(−z) is e⁰ = 1, so the output is 1 ÷ (1 + 1) = 0.5, which is halfway. The output approaches 0 only when z is large and negative.
At z = 0 the term e^(−z) is 1, so the output is 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. The output approaches 1 only when z is large and positive.

choices.label: Exactly halfway between 0 and 1
Close to 1
Close to 0

questions.prompt: A fully connected network has layer sizes 5, 2 and 1, with a bias on every neuron. How many parameters does it have?

questions.onCorrect: The count is 12 in the first layer and 3 in the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the first layer. The output layer has parameters too.
That counts the weights without the biases.

Then y = 3h − 4.

questions.onCorrect: The result equals 6x − 1 at x = 5, which shows that the two layers act as one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is h, the output of the first layer. The second layer still has to be applied.

questions.prompt: A first layer computes h = 3x − 2 and a second computes y = 2h + 5, with no activation between them. Which single rule gives the same output for every x?

questions.prompt: What is wrong with saying backpropagation and gradient descent are two alternative learning algorithms?

questions.prompt: A fully connected network has layer sizes 784, 128 and 10, with a bias on every neuron. How many parameters does it have?

misconceptions.feedback: Overfitting shows a high training score and a much lower validation score. Here both are low and the gap is only 0.02.
A small gap alone does not make a model good. Both scores are low, so the model has not learned the pattern even on the rows it was fitted to.

questions.prompt: A table has 4 numeric columns, a text column with 12 distinct levels and another text column with 5 distinct levels. Both text columns are one-hot encoded and replaced by their new columns. How many columns does the model receive?
hints: Each level of a text column becomes its own column.
The numeric columns stay as they are.
Add the new columns to the numeric ones.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 12-level column becomes 12 columns and the 5-level column becomes 5, so 12 + 5 = 17, and the 4 numeric columns make 21.

questions.onCorrect: Each text column becomes one column per level, and the numeric columns carry over unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 counts the columns before encoding: 4 numeric and 2 text. One-hot encoding gives each level its own column.
17 leaves out the 4 numeric columns, which the model still receives.
16 leaves out the 5-level column. Both text columns are encoded.

questions.prompt: A model predicts at dispatch time whether a parcel will arrive late, using the columns `distance_km`, `carrier`, `forecast_rain_mm` and `days_in_transit`. Which column leaks the label?
hints: Which column could only be filled in after the parcel has arrived?

acceptedIdeas: `days_in_transit`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `days_in_transit`

questions.onCorrect: The days in transit are known only once the parcel has arrived, so the column exists only for parcels whose outcome is already known.

choices.label: `distance_km`
`carrier`
`forecast_rain_mm`
`days_in_transit`

misconceptions.feedback: The distance is known when the parcel is booked, so it is available at dispatch time.
The carrier is chosen before dispatch, so it is available at prediction time.
A forecast is made before the parcel leaves, so it is known at prediction time.

questions.prompt: A node has 8 positive and 2 negative examples. What is its Gini impurity?
hints: The shares are 0.8 and 0.2.
Square each share and add the squares.
Subtract that sum from 1.
questions.onCorrect: The node is mostly one class, so its impurity of 0.32 sits well below the 0.5 of an even mix.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the squared shares. Gini is 1 minus that sum.
That is 0.8 × 0.2. Gini is 1 − 0.8² − 0.2², which is twice that product.

questions.prompt: A split on loan term sends 8 of the 10 loans to the left child, with a Gini of 0.375, and 2 loans to the right child, with a Gini of 0.5. What is the weighted child impurity?
hints: Each child counts in proportion to its share of the 10 loans.
The left child's share is 8 ÷ 10 and the right child's is 2 ÷ 10.
questions.onCorrect: The weighted impurity is 0.4, so the gain is 0.42 − 0.4 = 0.02. The loan-term question barely helps, and the tree would choose income, whose gain is 0.18, instead.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of the two Ginis. Each child counts in proportion to its share of the loans.
That adds the two Ginis without weighting them. Each child counts in proportion to its share of the loans.

questions.prompt: A tree grown until every leaf is pure scores 1.0 on its training rows and 0.78 on its validation rows. A tree limited to three levels scores 0.90 on training and 0.85 on validation. Which is likely to do better on new rows?
hints: Which of the two scores is measured on rows the tree was not fitted to?

acceptedIdeas: The shallow tree, because its validation accuracy is higher
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shallow tree, because its validation accuracy is higher

questions.onCorrect: The shallow tree does better on rows it did not fit. The deep tree has memorised noise, which is the high variance that bagging averages away.

choices.label: The deep tree, because its training accuracy is higher
The shallow tree, because its validation accuracy is higher
Both about equally, because each fits its training rows well

misconceptions.feedback: Training accuracy rewards memorising, and a perfect score is what a tree that has memorised its examples produces. The validation rows were never fitted, so they are the better guide.
The validation scores differ by seven points, and they are the ones measured on rows the trees never saw.

questions.prompt: The first bin's share fell from 0.4 to 0.3, so (a − e) is negative, yet its term is positive. Why is that?
hints: Work out the sign of ln(a ÷ e) when a is smaller than e.

acceptedIdeas: Both factors are negative, so their product is positive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both factors are negative, so their product is positive

questions.onCorrect: A fall in share makes both (a − e) and ln(a ÷ e) negative, so each bin's term is positive whichever way the share moved.

choices.label: ln(0.3 ÷ 0.4) is positive, because the ratio is a fraction
Both factors are negative, so their product is positive
The difference is squared, so a fall in share becomes positive

misconceptions.feedback: The logarithm of a number below 1 is negative. Here ln(0.75) is about −0.288.
The formula multiplies the difference by a logarithm and does not square it. The product is positive because both factors are negative.

questions.prompt: Two bins have expected shares 0.5 and 0.5 and actual shares 0.3 and 0.7. What is the second bin's term, (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e), to four decimal places?
hints: The difference a − e is 0.7 − 0.5.
The ratio a ÷ e is 0.7 ÷ 0.5 = 1.4.
Multiply the difference by the natural logarithm of the ratio.
questions.onCorrect: The two terms, 0.1022 and 0.0673, add to a PSI of 0.169, in the moderate range of the usual convention, between 0.1 and 0.25.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first bin's term. The second bin has risen, from 0.5 to 0.7.
That is ln(0.7 ÷ 0.5) alone. It still has to be multiplied by (a − e) = 0.2.

questions.prompt: A lender's applicants look the same as last year, but after a rise in interest rates the same income and debt now imply a higher chance of default. Which kind of change is this?
hints: Ask whether it is the inputs that moved or the meaning of the inputs.

acceptedIdeas: Concept drift
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Concept drift

questions.onCorrect: The inputs look the same, but what they imply for the label has changed, which is concept drift.

choices.label: Data drift only
Overfitting
Concept drift
Leakage

misconceptions.feedback: Data drift is a change in the inputs themselves. Here the applicants look the same and it is their relationship to the outcome that moved.
Overfitting is a property of how a model was fitted, and it does not come from the world changing later.
Leakage is information from the outcome entering the features, which this is not.

questions.prompt: A lender removes the applicant's age from its model's features but keeps the year in which each applicant first started work. Which statement is right?
hints: Ask whether another column could reveal age.

acceptedIdeas: The model can still use age, because the start year is correlated with it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The model can still use age, because the start year is correlated with it

questions.onCorrect: The start year stands in for age, so its effect remains, as a name or a postcode would stand in for another removed attribute.

choices.label: The model can no longer treat applicants differently by age
The model can still use age, because the start year is correlated with it
Per-group metrics by age can no longer be computed once the column is gone

misconceptions.feedback: A column that is correlated with age can carry the same information, so differences by age can survive.
The age column can be kept aside for auditing, so per-group metrics by age remain possible.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the gap, label minus prediction, between an example and a model's prediction for it?
flashcards.back: The residual is the label minus the prediction, so it is negative when the model predicts too high.

acceptedIdeas: residual
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: residual

flashcards.front: For the line ŷ = 2x + 1, what does the model predict for x = 3?
flashcards.back: Replace x with 3: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7.

flashcards.front: Why does a fitted line keep only two numbers, and what is lost?
flashcards.back: The line stores w and b and the individual examples are gone, so it describes the sample without proving a law.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the multiplier applied to the gradient in the update w ← w − η · gradient?
flashcards.back: The learning rate sets the length of each step, and too large a value makes the loss rise.

acceptedIdeas: learning rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: learning rate

flashcards.front: A model has one example, x = 2 and y = 6, loss ½(w·x − y)², and w = 1. What is the gradient x(w·x − y)?
flashcards.back: The residual is 2 − 6 = −4, and weighting it by x = 2 gives −8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The residual is 2 − 6 = −4, and weighting it by x = 2 gives −8.

flashcards.front: Why does gradient descent subtract the gradient instead of adding it?
flashcards.back: The gradient points in the direction in which the loss increases, so moving the opposite way lowers it.

flashcards.front: Of all the actual positives, the share the model finds is called what?
flashcards.back: Recall is TP ÷ (TP + FN), so it falls with every missed positive.

acceptedIdeas: recall
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: recall

flashcards.front: For TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20 and TN = 930, what is the recall, to three decimal places?
Why can a model with 97% accuracy still be poor?
flashcards.back: If positives are rare, a model that never predicts one can score nearly as high, so accuracy must be compared with the base rate.

flashcards.front: Which rate, the share of actual negatives that are flagged, is the horizontal axis of the ROC curve?
flashcards.back: The false positive rate is FP ÷ (FP + TN), and it rises as the threshold is lowered.

acceptedIdeas: false positive rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: false positive rate

flashcards.front: A model orders 45 of 60 positive-negative pairs correctly. What is its AUC?
flashcards.back: The AUC is the share of correctly ordered pairs: 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The AUC is the share of correctly ordered pairs: 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75.

flashcards.front: Why is an AUC of 0.9 not the same as 90% accuracy?
flashcards.back: The AUC counts correctly ordered positive-negative pairs across all thresholds, while accuracy counts correct decisions at one threshold.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a model whose training error is low and whose validation error is much higher?
flashcards.back: Overfitting means the model has matched the noise in its training examples and does not carry over to new data.

acceptedIdeas: overfitting
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: overfitting

flashcards.front: A model has training accuracy 0.95 and validation accuracy 0.78. What is the gap?
flashcards.back: The gap is the training score minus the validation score: 0.95 − 0.78 = 0.17.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The gap is the training score minus the validation score: 0.95 − 0.78 = 0.17.

flashcards.front: Why should the test set be used only once?
flashcards.back: Every choice made by looking at the test score leaks information from it, so repeated use makes the final score optimistic.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the error that comes from a model being too stiff to follow the pattern in the data?
flashcards.back: Bias is a consistent error from too simple a model, and it is balanced against variance by choosing a penalty strength.

acceptedIdeas: bias
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: bias

flashcards.front: Mean squared error 4, one parameter w = 1.5, penalty λ·w² with λ = 0.2. What is the penalised loss?
flashcards.back: The penalty is 0.2 × 2.25 = 0.45, so the loss is 4 + 0.45 = 4.45.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The penalty is 0.2 × 2.25 = 0.45, so the loss is 4 + 0.45 = 4.45.

flashcards.front: Why does cross-validation give an estimate for choosing a setting and not a finished model?
flashcards.back: The k fitted models are discarded after scoring, and the chosen setting is then used to fit a final model on all the training data.

flashcards.front: What is the name for information in the training data that will not be available when the model is used?
flashcards.back: Leakage lets the model see the answer or the test rows, so the evaluation overstates performance.

acceptedIdeas: leakage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: leakage

flashcards.front: For the values 0, 5 and 10, what is the min-max scaled value of 5?
Why must a scaler be fitted on the training rows only?
flashcards.back: Fitting it on every row lets the test rows influence the numbers, so the test score is no longer independent of the training.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the rows a bootstrap sample leaves out, used as a free validation set?
flashcards.back: The out-of-bag rows are about a third of the data for each tree, and they give an honest score without a separate validation set.

acceptedIdeas: out-of-bag
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: out-of-bag

flashcards.front: A node has 3 positive and 1 negative example. What is its Gini impurity?
Why does a vote of many trees help only if the trees differ?
flashcards.back: Identical trees make identical errors, so the majority is no better than one tree, while different trees make different errors that the vote outvotes.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the function, such as ReLU or sigmoid, that a neuron applies to its weighted sum?
flashcards.back: Without an activation, stacked layers would reduce to a single linear map.

acceptedIdeas: activation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: activation

flashcards.front: A layer has 6 inputs and 4 neurons, with a bias on each neuron. How many parameters does it have?
flashcards.back: The layer has 6 × 4 weights and 4 biases: 24 + 4 = 28.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The layer has 6 × 4 weights and 4 biases: 24 + 4 = 28.

flashcards.front: Why is an activation needed between layers?
flashcards.back: Without one, the layers multiply out to a single linear map, so extra layers add no power.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a fingerprint computed from the bytes of a file, used to identify a dataset in a run record?
flashcards.back: A hash changes completely if any byte changes, so it detects data that was altered.

acceptedIdeas: hash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: hash

flashcards.front: A search tries 4 learning rates and 5 depths with 3-fold cross-validation. How many fits is that?
flashcards.back: There are 4 × 5 = 20 configurations, and each is fitted on 3 folds: 60.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 4 × 5 = 20 configurations, and each is fitted on 3 folds: 60.

flashcards.front: Why is saving the model file not enough to reproduce a result?
flashcards.back: Without the code commit, the data version, the parameters, the seed and the environment, nobody can say what the model learned from or rebuild it.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a release stage in which a candidate model receives a copy of live traffic but its answers are never returned to users?
flashcards.back: A shadow deployment compares a candidate with the current model on real requests while no user sees the candidate's output.

acceptedIdeas: shadow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: shadow

flashcards.front: Peak 600 requests per second, 50 per replica, 60% target utilisation. How many replicas?
Why is passing offline evaluation not enough to ship a model?
flashcards.back: Production features can be computed differently from training features, and real traffic can differ from the test set, so a staged release has to check the model there.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a change in the relationship between the inputs and the label, so that the same features now imply a different outcome?
flashcards.back: Concept drift makes a model's learned rule out of date even when the input distributions have not moved.

acceptedIdeas: concept drift
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: concept drift

flashcards.front: Two bins have expected shares 0.5 and 0.5 and the same actual shares. What is the PSI?
flashcards.back: With no shift each term has (a − e) = 0, so the PSI is 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no shift each term has (a − e) = 0, so the PSI is 0.

flashcards.front: Why can stable accuracy fail to mean there is no drift?
flashcards.back: Labels may arrive late, so the accuracy shown describes old predictions, while the inputs may already have shifted.

flashcards.front: Which fairness measure compares the share of each group that receives the positive decision?
flashcards.back: Demographic parity asks selection rates to be equal across groups, which ignores who deserved the decision.

acceptedIdeas: demographic parity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: demographic parity

flashcards.front: Group M: 50 of 200 selected. Group N: 30 of 60 selected. What is the difference in selection rate, N minus M?
flashcards.back: M: 0.25 and N: 0.50, so the difference is 0.25.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: M: 0.25 and N: 0.50, so the difference is 0.25.

flashcards.front: Why does removing a protected attribute from the features not remove bias?
flashcards.back: Other features can be correlated with it and carry the same information, so the model recovers it and the bias in the labels comes through.
